Warehouse routing extends this: S might include (robot position, battery level, set of pending tasks), A includes navigation plus task-related actions (pick up, drop off, charge), and R reflects task completion, time efficiency, and battery management -- the STATE SPACE SIZE grows combinatorially with the number of tasks/robots, which is exactly where exact DP becomes infeasible and motivates the transition to function-approximation-based RL (covered in Deep RL).
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Dynamic Programmin.use_when: Use grid-world examples when LEARNING or TEACHING DP/RL concepts, or when UNIT-TESTING an algorithm implementation against a known-correct reference solution (e.g. 'does my Q-learning implementation converge to the same Q* that value iteration computes for this gridworld?'). Use warehouse-routing-style examples when motivating WHY real applications need to move beyond tabular methods, or when designing the state/action/reward structure for an actual fleet-management RL system (the gridworld intuitions about reward shaping, discount factor choice, and state design transfer directly, even though the algorithm changes).
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Dynamic Programmin.avoid_when: Don't extrapolate performance/behavior observed on toy grid worlds directly to real warehouse-scale problems without accounting for the SCALE GAP -- a DP or tabular RL approach that works perfectly on a 10x10 gridworld with 1 task doesn't 'just need more compute' to handle a warehouse with hundreds of cells, dozens of robots, and combinatorially many task assignments; the STATE SPACE EXPLOSION means a fundamentally different algorithmic approach (deep RL with function approximation, or even non-RL approaches like classical optimization/scheduling) is typically needed, not a scaled-up version of the same tabular method.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Dynamic Programmin.what_goes_wrong: A common pedagogical pitfall is presenting gridworld results as if they DIRECTLY demonstrate 'RL solves warehouse routing' -- in practice, many production warehouse-routing systems use classical operations-research techniques (vehicle routing problem solvers, constraint optimization) rather than RL, precisely because the combinatorial structure of multi-robot, multi-task routing has well-developed exact/near-exact OR solutions that don't require the sample-inefficient trial-and-error of RL. RL becomes more compelling for warehouse problems with elements that are HARD to model explicitly (e.g. learning to navigate around unpredictable human workers, or learning energy-efficient movement patterns) rather than for the core combinatorial assignment/routing problem itself -- conflating 'RL CAN be applied here' with 'RL is the BEST tool here' is a common overreach.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Dynamic Programmin.real_example: A training course teaches value iteration on a 5x5 gridworld, producing a clean visualization of V*(s) as a heatmap radiating outward from the goal, and π*(s) as arrows all pointing toward the goal along shortest paths -- students implement this in an afternoon and get a working, provably-optimal result. When the course then poses 'now extend this to a warehouse with 50 shelving units and 5 robots', students who naively try to extend the SAME tabular value-iteration code discover the state space (joint positions of 5 robots × task assignments × battery levels) has on the order of 10^15+ states -- value iteration's per-sweep cost (proportional to |S|) makes even ONE sweep computationally infeasible. This concrete scale comparison (5x5=25 states vs 10^15 states) is often used to viscerally motivate why DEEP RL (function approximation) or hybrid RL+OR approaches are necessary for realistic warehouse routing, rather than 'the same algorithm, just with a bigger computer'.

9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.what_it_is: Monte Carlo (MC) methods estimate value functions by averaging the ACTUAL RETURNS observed across many complete sampled episodes -- for each state (or state-action pair) visited, the MC estimate of V(s) (or Q(s,a)) is simply the average of G_t (the realized return from that visit to the end of the episode) across all visits, with no model of P or R required.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.why_it_exists: MC is the most DIRECT possible way to estimate E[G_t | S_t=s] -- if you can sample many trajectories starting from (or passing through) s and observe their actual returns, the sample average is an unbiased estimator of V^π(s) by the law of large numbers. It represents one extreme of the model-free spectrum (the other extreme being one-step TD): MC uses the FULL, ACTUAL return (zero bias, but high variance since a full episode's return depends on many random actions/transitions), while TD uses a one-step estimate (more bias from bootstrapping, but much lower variance).
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.how_it_works: After running an episode to completion (S_0,A_0,R_1,S_1,...,S_T), compute the return G_t for each visited state (working backward from the terminal state: G_T=0, G_t=R_{t+1}+γG_{t+1}). Update V(S_t) toward G_t -- either by maintaining running averages (V(s) = average of all G_t observed when in state s) or via an incremental update V(s)←V(s)+α[G_t-V(s)] (with constant α, giving more weight to recent episodes, useful for non-stationary problems). 'FIRST-VISIT' MC averages only the return from the FIRST time s is visited in each episode; 'EVERY-VISIT' MC averages returns from every visit -- both converge to V^π but have different statistical properties (first-visit gives i.i.d. samples, easier to analyze; every-visit samples are correlated within an episode but uses data more fully).
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.use_when: MC is appropriate when episodes are relatively SHORT (so waiting until episode end for an update isn't prohibitive) and TERMINATE reliably -- it's conceptually simple, UNBIASED (no bootstrapping error), and doesn't require the Markov property to hold as strictly as TD methods do for correctness (since it directly uses actual returns, not estimated successor values). It's also the basis for REINFORCE (the simplest policy gradient method), which is literally 'Monte Carlo policy gradient'.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.avoid_when: Avoid MC for CONTINUING tasks (no natural episode end) or VERY LONG episodes -- you must wait until an episode terminates before any update can be made, which means (a) no learning happens DURING long episodes, and (b) the variance of G_t (a sum of many random rewards) can be very high for long episodes, requiring many episodes to average out. TD methods, which update after every single step using bootstrapped estimates, avoid both issues at the cost of introducing bootstrapping bias.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.what_goes_wrong: A common implementation bug in first-visit MC is incorrectly identifying the 'first visit' to a state within an episode when a state can be revisited multiple times (e.g. an agent walking back and forth in a gridworld) -- using EVERY-VISIT logic while intending first-visit (or vice versa) changes the statistical properties of the estimator and can subtly bias results in environments with frequent state revisits, though both eventually converge given enough episodes. Another common issue is HIGH VARIANCE swamping the signal in environments with very long or highly stochastic episodes -- MC estimates can require orders of magnitude more episodes than TD to reach the same estimation accuracy, which is often misdiagnosed as 'the algorithm isn't learning' rather than 'the estimator has high variance and needs more samples'.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.real_example: A developer estimates V^π for a random policy in a gridworld using both first-visit MC and TD(0), running both for the same number of episodes -- the MC estimates for states near the START of typical episodes (visited early, with long remaining trajectories contributing to G_t) show much higher variance across independent runs (the estimated V(s) for the same state varies noticeably between different sets of 1000 episodes) compared to TD(0)'s estimates for the same states, which are more consistent run-to-run despite having some bootstrapping bias early in training. This variance-vs-bias trade-off is directly visible by comparing the SPREAD of estimates across multiple independent training runs, not just their average -- a useful diagnostic for understanding why TD methods are generally preferred for longer-horizon problems despite their bias.

9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.what_it_is: TD(0) is the simplest temporal-difference learning method -- it updates V(s) after EVERY SINGLE STEP using the one-step TD error: V(S_t) ← V(S_t) + α[R_{t+1} + γV(S_{t+1}) - V(S_t)], where the term R_{t+1}+γV(S_{t+1}) (called the 'TD target') is a one-step-bootstrapped estimate of G_t, and the difference (TD target - current estimate) is the 'TD error' δ_t.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.why_it_exists: TD(0) combines ideas from both Monte Carlo (learning from experience without a model, via sampling) and dynamic programming (bootstrapping -- using V(S_{t+1}) as a stand-in for the true future return, rather than waiting to observe it). This combination gives TD(0) a crucial practical advantage over MC: it can update its estimates AFTER EVERY STEP (no need to wait for episode completion), making it applicable to continuing tasks and giving much lower-variance updates (each update depends on only ONE random transition, not an entire trajectory) at the cost of introducing BOOTSTRAPPING BIAS (V(S_{t+1}) is itself an estimate, possibly inaccurate, especially early in training).
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.how_it_works: At each step, after observing (S_t, A_t, R_{t+1}, S_{t+1}), compute the TD error δ_t = R_{t+1} + γV(S_{t+1}) - V(S_t), and update V(S_t) ← V(S_t) + αδ_t. Intuitively: 'I thought state S_t was worth V(S_t); I just observed one step of real experience (reward R_{t+1}, landing in S_{t+1} which I currently think is worth V(S_{t+1})); adjust my estimate of S_t's value toward R_{t+1}+γV(S_{t+1}), by a small step α'. Over many steps/episodes, these small corrections propagate value information backward through the state space and converge (under standard step-size conditions) to V^π.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.use_when: TD(0) (and its generalizations, TD(λ), SARSA, Q-learning) is the default choice for most RL problems -- it works for both episodic and continuing tasks, updates online (every step), and generally has LOWER VARIANCE than MC, often leading to faster practical learning despite the bias. It's the foundation that essentially all modern value-based deep RL (DQN and descendants) builds on, just with V/Q represented by neural networks and updates done in batches from a replay buffer rather than single online steps.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.avoid_when: TD(0)'s bootstrapping means its updates depend on the CURRENT (possibly very inaccurate) estimate of V(S_{t+1}) -- early in training, when V is initialized arbitrarily (e.g. all zeros), TD targets are essentially noise propagating from equally-uninformed estimates, which can make EARLY learning slower to 'get going' compared to... actually, MC has the OPPOSITE early-training issue (correct but extremely noisy targets from real returns) -- in practice TD(0) usually still learns faster overall, but understanding that early TD targets are themselves built from poor estimates is important for interpreting early-training behavior (e.g. why value estimates can be temporarily WORSE before they improve, as errors initially propagate through an under-trained value function).
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.what_goes_wrong: The TD ERROR δ_t is one of the most diagnostically useful quantities in RL -- if δ_t remains large and doesn't shrink over training, it indicates the value function ISN'T CONVERGING (either the learning rate is too high causing oscillation, the function approximator lacks capacity/features to represent V^π accurately, or -- in deep RL -- the bootstrapped target itself is a MOVING TARGET that the network is chasing without ever catching up, motivating target networks). A common debugging step when a deep RL agent's value loss plateaus at a non-trivial value (rather than decreasing toward near-zero) is examining whether the TD errors are systematically biased in a particular direction (e.g. consistently positive, suggesting systematic underestimation) vs. just noisy (suggesting an inherent stochasticity/variance floor).
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.real_example: A developer compares TD(0) and MC for estimating V^π in a gridworld with γ=0.9, plotting the estimation error (vs. the ground-truth V^π from value iteration) over training episodes for both methods, averaged across multiple independent runs -- TD(0) converges faster on average (lower error after a fixed number of episodes) but exhibits a small persistent BIAS early on (its estimates for states far from the goal are initially too close to zero, since the bootstrapped target from an equally-near-zero V(S_{t+1}) hasn't yet 'learned' that distant states have nonzero value), while MC has higher VARIANCE (estimates for the same state fluctuate more across independent runs) but no systematic bias. This bias-variance trade-off, visualized directly, is the canonical illustration of TD vs MC.

9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.what_it_is: TD(λ) is a family of algorithms parameterized by λ ∈ [0,1] that smoothly INTERPOLATES between TD(0) (λ=0, one-step bootstrapping) and Monte Carlo (λ=1, full-episode returns), using ELIGIBILITY TRACES -- a mechanism that tracks how 'eligible' each state is for credit/blame from the current TD error, based on how recently it was visited.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.why_it_exists: TD(0) and MC sit at two extremes of a bias-variance trade-off (TD(0): low variance, more bias from one-step bootstrapping; MC: unbiased, high variance from full-episode returns). TD(λ) exists to let practitioners choose an INTERMEDIATE point on this spectrum -- intermediate λ values often achieve better overall learning performance than either extreme, by using multi-step (but not full-episode) information to form targets, weighted by an exponentially-decaying combination of n-step returns (this is the λ-return, equivalent in expectation to a particular weighted average of all n-step returns for n=1,2,3,...).
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.how_it_works: An ELIGIBILITY TRACE e(s) is maintained for every state, initialized to 0, and updated at each step: e(S_t) ← e(S_t) + 1 (the just-visited state becomes maximally eligible), and ALL traces decay: e(s) ← γλ·e(s) for all s (recently-visited states remain somewhat eligible, decaying geometrically with rate γλ). When a TD error δ_t = R_{t+1}+γV(S_{t+1})-V(S_t) is computed, EVERY state s has its value updated proportionally to its current eligibility: V(s) ← V(s) + αδ_t·e(s) -- so the 'blame/credit' for a single TD error is distributed across recently-visited states, with more-recently-visited states (higher e(s)) getting more credit. This achieves, in an ONLINE, incremental way, an effect equivalent to weighting n-step returns by (1-λ)λ^{n-1} -- λ=0 collapses to pure 1-step TD (only the just-visited state gets credit), λ=1 approaches MC-like full-return credit assignment.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.use_when: TD(λ) with intermediate λ (e.g. 0.8-0.95) is useful when you want FASTER CREDIT PROPAGATION than TD(0) provides (where information about a delayed reward takes many episodes to 'back up' one step at a time to earlier states) without the full variance of MC -- it's particularly valuable in environments with DELAYED REWARDS (the consequence of an action is only revealed many steps later), where TD(0)'s one-step-at-a-time backup is slow to propagate that information backward through the visited states.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.avoid_when: TD(λ) (with the classic eligibility-trace formulation) has become LESS COMMON in modern deep RL, where its role is often played instead by n-step returns with a fixed n (simpler to implement with experience replay/batched training) or by Generalised Advantage Estimation (GAE, which is conceptually a λ-return applied to ADVANTAGES rather than values, used in PPO/TRPO). Eligibility traces are awkward to combine with experience replay (the trace mechanism assumes a single ongoing trajectory, while replay samples i.i.d. transitions from a buffer) -- for replay-based deep RL, n-step returns or GAE are typically preferred over literal eligibility traces.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.what_goes_wrong: A common confusion is treating λ as if it were INDEPENDENT of γ in its effect on the 'effective horizon' of credit assignment -- the trace decay rate is γλ (the PRODUCT), so the same λ has very different practical effects depending on γ: with γ=0.99, λ=0.9 gives a trace decay of 0.891 (still fairly long credit-assignment horizon), while with γ=0.9, the same λ=0.9 gives a trace decay of 0.81 (shorter). Tuning λ in isolation without considering its interaction with γ can lead to confusing results when γ is changed for other reasons (e.g. adjusting the task horizon) but λ is left at its old value, inadvertently changing the credit-assignment horizon as a side effect.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.real_example: In a delayed-reward gridworld (reward of +1 only at the very end of a 50-step episode, 0 otherwise, γ=0.99), TD(0) takes many hundreds of episodes for V(s) for STARTING states to become noticeably nonzero, because the +1 reward signal must propagate backward ONE STATE PER EPISODE through the one-step TD updates. Using TD(λ) with λ=0.9 (trace decay γλ≈0.89), the same +1 terminal reward immediately updates V(s) for MANY recently-visited states within a SINGLE episode (each state along the trajectory has nonzero eligibility when the terminal TD error arrives), dramatically speeding up the propagation of this delayed-reward signal -- visually, V(s) for states throughout the gridworld becomes informative within tens of episodes rather than hundreds.

9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.what_it_is: SARSA (State-Action-Reward-State-Action) is the TD-control algorithm that learns Q^π for the policy π the agent is ACTUALLY FOLLOWING (including its exploration behavior) -- its update rule is Q(S_t,A_t) ← Q(S_t,A_t) + α[R_{t+1} + γQ(S_{t+1},A_{t+1}) - Q(S_t,A_t)], where A_{t+1} is the action the agent ACTUALLY TAKES next (sampled from its current, typically exploratory, policy) -- hence the name, from the quintuple (S_t,A_t,R_{t+1},S_{t+1},A_{t+1}).
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.why_it_exists: SARSA is the natural TD-control analog of policy-evaluation-then-improvement: it estimates the action-value of the CURRENT (behavior) policy, which can then be improved (e.g. via ε-greedy with respect to the learned Q). Being ON-POLICY -- learning about the policy that's actually generating the data, INCLUDING its exploration noise -- gives SARSA a distinct character from Q-learning: it learns a policy that accounts for the RISK of its own exploratory actions, which can matter in environments where exploration itself can be costly or dangerous.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.how_it_works: At each step, the agent is in state S_t, takes action A_t (chosen by its current ε-greedy-or-similar policy), observes R_{t+1} and S_{t+1}, then SELECTS THE NEXT ACTION A_{t+1} (again via its current policy, BEFORE the update), and updates Q(S_t,A_t) toward R_{t+1}+γQ(S_{t+1},A_{t+1}) -- the TD target uses the Q-value of the action the agent will ACTUALLY take, not the best possible action. Because A_{t+1} might be an exploratory (non-greedy) action, SARSA's targets incorporate the CONSEQUENCES of exploration into the learned Q-values.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.use_when: Use SARSA when the COST OF EXPLORATION matters and should be reflected in the learned values -- the canonical example is the 'Cliff Walking' gridworld, where SARSA learns a SAFER path that stays away from a cliff edge (because its ε-greedy exploration occasionally causes it to step off the cliff near the edge, and SARSA's on-policy targets incorporate this risk into Q-values for near-edge states), while Q-learning learns the OPTIMAL (edge-hugging, shortest) path assuming purely greedy behavior, which is riskier under actual ε-greedy execution.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.avoid_when: Don't use SARSA when you specifically want to learn the value of the OPTIMAL policy independent of the exploration strategy used during training (e.g. if exploration is just a means to gather data, and you'll deploy a purely greedy policy at test time) -- in that case, Q-learning's off-policy nature (learning Q* regardless of the exploratory behavior policy) is more directly aligned with the deployment objective. SARSA's learned values are tied to ITS OWN exploration schedule -- if ε changes over training (e.g. annealed toward 0), SARSA is technically learning a MOVING TARGET (Q^{π_ε} for a changing ε), which complicates convergence analysis compared to Q-learning's fixed target Q*.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.what_goes_wrong: A common bug when implementing SARSA (vs Q-learning) is forgetting that A_{t+1} must be SELECTED BEFORE the update and REUSED as the actual next action taken (not re-sampled) -- if A_{t+1} is sampled twice (once for the update's TD target, and again -- independently -- as the action actually executed at the next step), the algorithm becomes a hybrid that doesn't correspond exactly to either SARSA or Expected SARSA, and its theoretical on-policy guarantees no longer cleanly apply. This is an easy mistake when refactoring Q-learning code (which doesn't need to 'pre-select' the next action, since it uses max) into SARSA.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.real_example: On the classic Cliff Walking gridworld (a long cliff edge with large negative reward for falling off, goal at the far end), training both SARSA and Q-learning with the SAME ε-greedy exploration (ε=0.1) for the same number of episodes produces visibly different LEARNED POLICIES when later evaluated WITH ε=0.1 still active (i.e., during ongoing exploration): SARSA's policy takes a path one row away from the cliff edge (sacrificing a couple of extra steps to reduce the chance that an exploratory action causes a fall), while Q-learning's policy hugs the cliff edge (the objectively shortest path, optimal for a purely greedy policy, but riskier under ε-greedy execution -- Q-learning doesn't account for ITS OWN exploration noise in its targets). This is the canonical example used to teach the practical difference between on-policy and off-policy TD control.

9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.what_it_is: Q-learning is the TD-control algorithm that directly estimates Q* (the OPTIMAL action-value function), regardless of what policy is actually generating the training data -- its update rule is Q(S_t,A_t) ← Q(S_t,A_t) + α[R_{t+1} + γ max_{a'}Q(S_{t+1},a') - Q(S_t,A_t)], using max over the next state's Q-values (the Bellman OPTIMALITY target) rather than the Q-value of whatever action is actually taken next.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.why_it_exists: Q-learning is OFF-POLICY: the policy being learned about (implicitly, the greedy policy with respect to Q, which converges to π*) can differ from the BEHAVIOR policy generating the experience (e.g. an ε-greedy policy for exploration). This separation is enormously practically useful -- it means you can explore however you like (even very randomly) while STILL learning about the optimal policy, and it's the foundation for EXPERIENCE REPLAY (reusing old data collected under old, different policies is valid for off-policy methods but not, without correction, for strictly on-policy methods) -- which is essential to DQN and its descendants.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.how_it_works: At each step, observe (S_t,A_t,R_{t+1},S_{t+1}) -- the action A_t can come from ANY exploration strategy. Compute the TD target using max_{a'}Q(S_{t+1},a') -- 'assume I'll act optimally (greedily w.r.t. my current Q estimate) from S_{t+1} onward', regardless of what action is actually taken next. Update Q(S_t,A_t) toward this target. Because the target doesn't depend on the actual next action taken, Q-learning can learn from transitions generated by ARBITRARY policies (including past, outdated policies, as in experience replay) -- this is what 'off-policy' means in practice: the data-generating distribution can differ from the distribution implicitly being evaluated/improved.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.use_when: Q-learning (and its deep RL descendant, DQN) is the right choice when you want to learn Q* (and hence π*) and don't need the learned values to reflect the SPECIFIC exploration strategy used -- which is the typical deployment scenario (explore during training, deploy a greedy/near-greedy policy at test time). Its off-policy nature also makes it compatible with experience replay, multi-step returns computed from old data, and offline RL (learning entirely from a fixed dataset of past experience, without any new interaction) -- all scenarios where on-policy methods would require importance-sampling corrections or simply don't apply.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.avoid_when: Don't use vanilla tabular Q-learning's max-based update with FUNCTION APPROXIMATION (large neural networks) without additional stabilization -- the combination of (1) bootstrapping (target depends on current network's own estimates), (2) function approximation (updates to one state's Q-value can affect estimates for OTHER states via shared parameters), and (3) the max operator's overestimation bias creates a notoriously unstable combination (sometimes called the 'deadly triad') -- this is precisely why DQN required experience replay AND target networks to work at all, and why naive 'Q-learning with a neural network' often diverges.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.what_goes_wrong: Beyond the overestimation bias (covered in the Bellman optimality note), a subtle off-policy issue is that Q-learning's CONVERGENCE GUARANTEE (in the tabular case) requires that ALL state-action pairs continue to be visited infinitely often during training -- if the exploration policy becomes too greedy too quickly (ε decayed to near-0 before Q has converged), some state-action pairs may stop being visited while their Q-values are still inaccurate, and these inaccurate values can persist indefinitely (never corrected, since they're never revisited) -- producing a policy that's confidently wrong about rarely-visited states/actions, often discovered only when the agent is later forced into one of these states (e.g. by a distribution shift at deployment) and behaves erratically.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.real_example: A tabular Q-learning agent for a gridworld with ε decayed linearly from 1.0 to 0.01 over the first 100 episodes (out of 1000 total) converges to a policy that performs near-optimally on the MAIN paths through the gridworld, but a rarely-visited corner cell (only reachable via a specific sequence of early, highly-exploratory actions that became unlikely after ε dropped) retains its INITIAL (zero) Q-values for all actions, never updated after ε became too small to revisit it. When the environment is later slightly modified (a shortcut near that corner is added, making it newly relevant), the agent's policy doesn't discover or exploit the shortcut -- its stale, never-updated Q-values for that corner make it look unattractive compared to the well-explored main path, even though it's now objectively better. Extending the high-ε exploration phase (or using a more sophisticated exploration schedule) ensures all relevant states get adequately explored before ε decays.

9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.what_it_is: Expected SARSA is a TD-control variant whose update rule replaces SARSA's Q(S_{t+1},A_{t+1}) (the Q-value of the SPECIFIC next action actually taken) with the EXPECTATION over the policy's action distribution: Q(S_t,A_t) ← Q(S_t,A_t) + α[R_{t+1} + γ Σ_{a'}π(a'|S_{t+1})Q(S_{t+1},a') - Q(S_t,A_t)] -- it computes the FULL expected value of the next state under the current policy, rather than sampling a single next action.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.why_it_exists: Expected SARSA addresses a specific weakness of plain SARSA: SARSA's target Q(S_{t+1},A_{t+1}) depends on which SPECIFIC action A_{t+1} happens to be sampled from the (often stochastic, e.g. ε-greedy) policy -- this introduces additional VARIANCE into the target beyond what's inherent to the environment, since the SAME (S_t,A_t,R_{t+1},S_{t+1}) could produce different targets depending on which A_{t+1} gets sampled. Expected SARSA REMOVES this extra source of variance by averaging over ALL possible next actions weighted by their probability under π, at the cost of a small additional computation (a sum over the action space) per update.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.how_it_works: Given (S_t,A_t,R_{t+1},S_{t+1}), instead of sampling A_{t+1} and using Q(S_{t+1},A_{t+1}) in the target (as SARSA does), Expected SARSA computes Σ_{a'}π(a'|S_{t+1})Q(S_{t+1},a') -- for an ε-greedy policy with |A| actions, this is (1-ε)·max_a Q(S_{t+1},a) + (ε/|A|)·Σ_a Q(S_{t+1},a) (the greedy action gets probability 1-ε plus its share of the ε exploration mass, every other action gets ε/|A|). Note that with ε=0 (purely greedy policy), Expected SARSA's target reduces EXACTLY to Q-learning's max_a Q(S_{t+1},a) -- Expected SARSA can be seen as a GENERALIZATION that smoothly interpolates between SARSA-like on-policy behavior (for ε>0) and Q-learning-like behavior (as ε→0), while always being on-policy with respect to whatever π is currently being followed.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.use_when: Expected SARSA is generally a STRICT IMPROVEMENT over plain SARSA for small/discrete action spaces -- the extra computation (summing over |A| actions) is cheap when |A| is small, and the variance reduction typically leads to faster, more stable learning. It's a good default 'on-policy TD control' choice for tabular or small-action-space problems where SARSA would otherwise be used.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.avoid_when: For LARGE or CONTINUOUS action spaces, computing Σ_{a'}π(a'|S_{t+1})Q(S_{t+1},a') exactly becomes expensive or impossible (the sum/integral over actions has no closed form for arbitrary Q) -- this is the same scalability issue that affects Q-learning's max_a operator, and is why continuous-action methods don't use Expected-SARSA-style updates directly; they instead rely on the actor network as an implicit, learned approximation to the relevant expectation/max.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.what_goes_wrong: A subtle but important point: Expected SARSA's reduced variance comes from REMOVING the randomness of WHICH action A_{t+1} is sampled, but it does NOT remove the inherent randomness of the ENVIRONMENT's transition S_{t+1} (which is still sampled, just once, as in SARSA/Q-learning) -- conflating 'Expected SARSA has lower variance' with 'Expected SARSA is variance-free' can lead to unrealistic expectations about how quickly it converges in highly stochastic environments. The variance reduction from Expected SARSA is typically modest in practice (one less source of randomness among several), not transformative -- it's a genuine but incremental improvement, not a different order of method.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.real_example: Comparing SARSA and Expected SARSA on a gridworld with ε=0.3 (fairly high exploration rate, amplifying SARSA's extra variance from sampling A_{t+1}), both algorithms converge to similar final Q-value estimates, but Expected SARSA's learning curve (Q-value estimates vs. training steps, averaged over multiple runs) is visibly SMOOTHER with a narrower confidence band across runs -- particularly for states where the ε-greedy policy's non-greedy actions have very different Q-values from the greedy action (high 'spread' among Σ_a Q(s',a) terms), which is exactly where SARSA's single-sample A_{t+1} introduces the most additional variance into its target compared to Expected SARSA's full expectation.

9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.what_it_is: n-step returns generalize the TD-target spectrum by bootstrapping after n steps instead of 1 (TD(0)) or ∞ (Monte Carlo): G_t^{(n)} = R_{t+1} + γR_{t+2} + ... + γ^{n-1}R_{t+n} + γ^n V(S_{t+n}) -- the first n actual rewards are used directly, and the remaining (infinite-tail) return is approximated by the bootstrapped value estimate V(S_{t+n}).
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.why_it_exists: n-step returns provide a simple, TUNABLE knob for the bias-variance trade-off between TD(0) (n=1: low variance, more bootstrapping bias) and MC (n=∞: unbiased, high variance) -- without needing the more complex machinery of eligibility traces (TD(λ)). In deep RL, n-step returns are popular precisely because they're easy to implement with experience replay/batched training: just store n consecutive transitions and compute the n-step sum, no per-step trace updates needed.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.how_it_works: Given a sequence of n transitions starting from S_t, compute the n-step return by summing the discounted actual rewards R_{t+1} through R_{t+n}, then add γ^n times the CURRENT value estimate of the state n steps ahead, V(S_{t+n}) (or Q(S_{t+n},A_{t+n}) for control). The update is V(S_t) ← V(S_t) + α[G_t^{(n)} - V(S_t)] (or the Q-learning/SARSA analog). Larger n means MORE of the return comes from actual observed rewards (less bias from bootstrapping at an early, possibly-inaccurate value estimate) but ALSO more accumulated variance from those n random rewards.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.use_when: n-step returns (with n typically in the 3-10 range, sometimes higher) are widely used in modern deep RL -- e.g. Rainbow DQN uses multi-step (n-step) returns as one of its component improvements, and many policy-gradient/actor-critic implementations use n-step returns or GAE (a related, more sophisticated multi-step technique) for computing advantage estimates. They're particularly useful when single-step bootstrapping is too slow to propagate reward information (similar motivation to TD(λ)), but the eligibility-trace machinery is inconvenient (e.g. with replay buffers).
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.avoid_when: Very large n approaches Monte-Carlo-like variance, which can destabilize learning especially with FUNCTION APPROXIMATION (where high-variance targets can cause large, noisy gradient updates). Also, n-step returns computed from a REPLAY BUFFER under OFF-POLICY learning have a subtle issue: the n actual rewards R_{t+1}...R_{t+n} were generated by WHATEVER POLICY was in effect when that data was collected, but the bootstrapped tail V(S_{t+n}) uses the CURRENT value function -- this mixing of 'old-policy actual rewards' with 'current-policy bootstrap' introduces an off-policy bias that grows with n (since more of the return comes from old-policy rewards) unless corrected (e.g. via importance sampling, or simply accepting the bias as 'good enough' for moderate n, which is common practice in algorithms like Rainbow/Ape-X).
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.what_goes_wrong: A common implementation detail that's easy to get wrong is handling EPISODE BOUNDARIES within the n-step window -- if the episode terminates at step t+k for k<n (before the full n-step window is observed), the return must be truncated to NOT include a bootstrapped tail (since the terminal state has V=0 and no future) -- i.e., G_t^{(k)} = R_{t+1}+...+γ^{k-1}R_{t+k} with NO +γ^k V(S_{t+k}) term, because S_{t+k} is terminal. Implementations that naively always add a bootstrap term regardless of episode termination introduce a systematic error for transitions near episode ends, which can be especially problematic for episodes with informative terminal rewards (the bootstrap term incorrectly adds 'phantom' future value to a state that has none).
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.real_example: An Ape-X-style distributed RL implementation uses n=3 step returns computed from a replay buffer -- a bug in the buffer's sampling logic doesn't check for episode boundaries when constructing 3-step windows, so for transitions within the last 2 steps of an episode, the computed 'return' incorrectly includes rewards and a bootstrap value from the FOLLOWING episode (which started from a reset state, unrelated to the current trajectory). This manifests as occasional anomalously large or small Q-value targets for terminal-adjacent states, visible as outlier spikes in the TD-error distribution -- fixed by truncating the n-step window (and omitting the bootstrap term) whenever a 'done' flag is encountered within the window.

9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.what_it_is: These are three foundational strategies for balancing exploration (trying actions to gather information) and exploitation (taking the currently-best-known action): ε-GREEDY takes the greedy (best-known) action with probability 1-ε and a uniformly random action with probability ε; UCB (Upper Confidence Bound) selects the action maximizing an OPTIMISTIC estimate (estimated value PLUS a bonus for uncertainty -- actions tried less often get a larger bonus); THOMPSON SAMPLING maintains a probability distribution over each action's value, samples one value per action from these distributions, and picks the action with the highest sampled value.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.why_it_exists: Without SOME exploration mechanism, an agent that's purely greedy from the start can get permanently stuck exploiting a suboptimal action it happened to try first (if its initial estimate looked good by chance), never discovering better alternatives. These three strategies represent increasingly SOPHISTICATED ways of managing the explore/exploit trade-off: ε-greedy is simple but explores UNIFORMLY at random (wasting exploration on clearly-bad actions); UCB and Thompson sampling both explore MORE INTELLIGENTLY, directing exploration toward actions whose VALUE IS UNCERTAIN (rather than actions known to be bad), which is provably more sample-efficient in bandit settings.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.how_it_works: ε-GREEDY: with probability ε (often annealed from high to low over training), pick a uniformly random action; otherwise pick argmax_a Q(s,a) -- simple, but spends exploration budget equally on all non-greedy actions regardless of how promising they look. UCB: pick argmax_a [Q(s,a) + c·sqrt(ln(t)/N(s,a))] -- the bonus term grows with total time t and shrinks with N(s,a) (how often action a has been tried), so RARELY-TRIED actions get a larger 'benefit of the doubt' bonus, naturally directing exploration toward under-explored actions while still favoring high-Q actions. THOMPSON SAMPLING: maintain a posterior distribution (e.g. Beta distribution for Bernoulli rewards) over each action's expected reward, SAMPLE one value from each action's posterior, and act greedily with respect to these samples -- actions with high uncertainty (wide posteriors) occasionally produce high samples (encouraging exploration), while actions with confidently-low estimates rarely produce competitive samples.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.use_when: ε-greedy remains the most common choice in DEEP RL (DQN and descendants) due to its simplicity and compatibility with arbitrary value-function representations -- it's a reasonable default, especially with an annealing schedule (high ε early, low ε later). UCB and Thompson sampling are more common in MULTI-ARMED BANDIT settings (and contextual bandits, e.g. recommendation systems, A/B testing with adaptive allocation) where the action set is small/fixed and the stronger theoretical guarantees (regret bounds) and sample efficiency matter more, and where maintaining per-action uncertainty estimates (counts for UCB, posteriors for Thompson sampling) is tractable.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.avoid_when: UCB and Thompson sampling, in their classic forms, assume a relatively small, STATIONARY (or slowly-changing) action set with trackable per-action statistics (counts, posteriors) -- they don't naturally extend to the LARGE STATE SPACES of typical deep RL (you'd need per-state-action counts/posteriors, which for continuous/high-dimensional state spaces is as intractable as a Q-table). This is why deep RL predominantly uses ε-greedy (or related simple noise-injection methods like adding Gaussian noise to continuous actions, or entropy bonuses in policy gradient methods) rather than UCB/Thompson-sampling-style exploration, despite the latter's theoretical advantages in simpler settings.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.what_goes_wrong: A common ε-greedy mistake is using a FIXED ε throughout training (e.g. always ε=0.1) -- this means even a FULLY CONVERGED, optimal policy still takes a random (possibly bad) action 10% of the time FOREVER, which both wastes performance at deployment (if the same ε-greedy policy is used for evaluation) and can be DANGEROUS in safety-critical settings (a converged self-driving policy that still takes random actions 10% of the time is unacceptable). The standard fix is ANNEALING ε over training (e.g. linearly from 1.0 to 0.01 over the first N steps) and using a near-zero or zero ε at evaluation/deployment time -- forgetting this distinction between TRAINING exploration and EVALUATION/deployment behavior is a frequent source of 'why does my trained agent still act randomly sometimes' confusion.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.real_example: A contextual bandit system for website A/B testing (choosing which of 5 page layouts to show each visitor to maximize click-through rate) initially uses ε-greedy with ε=0.1 -- after substantial traffic, 4 of the 5 layouts are clearly worse, yet the system continues showing them to 2% of visitors each (ε/5) indefinitely, representing a real, ongoing cost (worse layouts shown to real users) with no benefit (their relative ranking was determined long ago and isn't changing). Switching to Thompson sampling (maintaining a Beta posterior over each layout's click-through rate, sampling and acting greedily w.r.t. samples) causes exploration of clearly-worse layouts to NATURALLY TAPER OFF over time (their posteriors become tight and low, rarely producing competitive samples) while still automatically re-exploring if a layout's performance later changes (posterior remains responsive to new data) -- achieving better overall click-through rate than fixed-ε ε-greedy, with no manual annealing schedule needed.

9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.what_it_is: The exploitation-exploration trade-off is the fundamental tension in any RL (or bandit) problem between EXPLOITING current knowledge (taking the action believed to be best, to maximize immediate reward) and EXPLORING (taking other actions to gather information that might reveal a BETTER action, at the cost of potentially lower immediate reward) -- it's a tension that exists in essentially every sequential decision-making problem under uncertainty, not just RL.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.why_it_exists: An agent's knowledge of action values is always based on LIMITED experience, and that knowledge could be wrong -- an action that looks suboptimal based on current (limited) data might actually be optimal, but the agent will never discover this without trying it. Pure exploitation risks getting permanently stuck on a suboptimal action (if early, noisy estimates happened to favor it); pure exploration wastes reward on actions known/suspected to be bad. The trade-off EXISTS because there's no way to simultaneously maximize 'reward right now, given current knowledge' and 'information gained about the environment' -- every action is either fully one or a mix of both, and the right balance depends on factors like how much time remains, how uncertain current estimates are, and how costly exploration is.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.how_it_works: Formally, this trade-off is most cleanly studied in the MULTI-ARMED BANDIT setting (a simplified RL problem with one state and k actions, each with an unknown reward distribution) -- the goal is to minimize REGRET (the cumulative difference between the reward obtained and the reward an oracle with perfect knowledge would have obtained). Different exploration strategies (ε-greedy, UCB, Thompson sampling, covered separately) achieve different REGRET BOUNDS -- e.g. UCB and Thompson sampling achieve LOGARITHMIC regret (regret grows as O(log T) with the number of pulls T), while ε-greedy with constant ε achieves only LINEAR regret (since it keeps exploring at a constant rate forever) -- annealed ε-greedy can achieve better bounds but requires careful schedule tuning. In full RL (multi-state), the trade-off is compounded by the fact that exploration in one state can affect what's REACHABLE/learnable in other states.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.use_when: Thinking explicitly about this trade-off matters whenever you're choosing or tuning an exploration strategy, or diagnosing why an agent seems 'stuck' -- if an agent converges to a policy that's clearly suboptimal and STAYS THERE (doesn't improve with more training), insufficient exploration (premature convergence to exploitation) is a prime suspect; if an agent's performance is noisy and never stabilizes even late in training, EXCESSIVE exploration (too much randomness even when good actions are well-identified) is a prime suspect.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.avoid_when: Don't treat the explore/exploit trade-off as something to 'solve once' with a fixed exploration strategy/schedule and never revisit -- the RIGHT amount of exploration depends on the task's reward structure (sparse rewards generally need MORE exploration to ever encounter reward signal at all) and can change as training progresses (early training generally needs more exploration than late training, but the right RATE of decay is task-dependent) -- a schedule tuned for one task/reward-structure often transfers poorly to a different task, and exploration hyperparameters are frequently among the most impactful (and most under-tuned) knobs in an RL project.
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.what_goes_wrong: PREMATURE CONVERGENCE -- the agent settles into a LOCAL OPTIMUM policy early in training (often because early exploration happened to make this policy look good, and insufficient subsequent exploration prevents discovering better alternatives) -- is one of the most common and hardest-to-diagnose RL failure modes, because the training curve LOOKS like successful convergence (reward plateaus at a stable, non-trivial value) -- it's indistinguishable from TRUE convergence to a good policy without either (a) domain knowledge about what performance SHOULD be achievable, or (b) deliberately increasing exploration (e.g. temporarily raising ε, or adding intrinsic-motivation bonuses) and checking whether performance subsequently improves (if it does, the original 'convergence' was premature).
9|🟡 T2 RL Foundations|Model-Free Methods.real_example: An agent trained on a sparse-reward maze (reward only upon reaching the exit, which requires a specific sequence of turns including one COUNTERINTUITIVE detour away from the apparent direction of the goal) converges after a few thousand episodes to a policy that consistently reaches a DEAD END close to (but not at) the goal, achieving zero reward but doing so 'consistently' -- the training curve (average reward) is flat at zero, which could mean either 'hasn't learned anything yet' or 'stuck in a local behavioral pattern'. The team adds a curiosity-based intrinsic reward (bonus for visiting novel states) for an additional training phase -- the agent's behavior immediately becomes more varied, it discovers the counterintuitive detour, finds the exit, and the TRUE reward signal finally becomes available, after which standard training (without the intrinsic bonus) converges to a good policy. This illustrates that a flat reward curve at zero can mask 'stuck due to insufficient exploration' vs. 'hasn't found the solution structure yet' -- both look identical from the reward curve alone.

9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Deep.what_it_is: DQN (Deep Q-Network) is the algorithm that combines Q-learning with a deep neural network as the Q-function approximator -- Q(s,a;θ), parameterized by network weights θ, takes a state (e.g. raw pixels) as input and outputs Q-values for each discrete action. DQN (DeepMind, 2015) was the first algorithm to achieve human-level performance on a range of Atari games directly from pixel input, and it's the foundational algorithm for essentially all subsequent value-based deep RL.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Deep.why_it_exists: Tabular Q-learning requires a separate Q-value for every (state, action) pair -- infeasible for high-dimensional state spaces like images (a single Atari frame has ~256^(84*84) possible pixel configurations). Neural networks provide FUNCTION APPROXIMATION: a single network with a manageable number of parameters can generalize across the (effectively infinite) state space, outputting reasonable Q-values even for states never exactly seen before. However, naively combining Q-learning's bootstrapped, off-policy update with a neural network is UNSTABLE (the 'deadly triad' of bootstrapping + function approximation + off-policy data) -- DQN's specific contributions (experience replay and target networks, covered separately) are what made this combination WORK in practice.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Deep.how_it_works: The network Q(s,a;θ) is trained by minimizing the squared TD error: L(θ) = E[(r + γ max_{a'}Q(s',a';θ⁻) - Q(s,a;θ))²], where θ⁻ are the parameters of a separate TARGET NETWORK (a periodically-updated copy of θ, covered in its own note) -- this is just Q-learning's update rule, but expressed as a LOSS FUNCTION minimized via gradient descent (specifically, stochastic gradient descent on mini-batches sampled from an EXPERIENCE REPLAY buffer, also covered separately) rather than applied as a per-state table update. For Atari, the input is a stack of recent raw pixel frames (to partially address the Markov-property issue -- a single frame doesn't show velocity/direction), processed by convolutional layers, feeding into fully-connected layers that output one Q-value per discrete action (e.g. 18 joystick/button combinations).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Deep.use_when: DQN (or its modern successors -- Double DQN, Dueling DQN, Rainbow) is the standard starting point for DISCRETE-ACTION RL problems with high-dimensional observations (images, large state vectors) -- it's well-understood, has many stable open-source implementations (Stable-Baselines3, CleanRL, RLlib), and serves as a solid baseline before considering more complex algorithms.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Deep.avoid_when: DQN's core max_a Q(s,a;θ) operation requires ENUMERATING all actions, which is natural for small discrete action spaces but doesn't extend to continuous action spaces (covered by DDPG/TD3/SAC instead) or extremely large discrete action spaces (where enumerating all actions per forward pass becomes a bottleneck -- specialized architectures or action-embedding approaches are needed). Also, vanilla DQN is notoriously SAMPLE-INEFFICIENT (often requiring tens of millions of environment steps for Atari-level tasks) -- for problems where environment interaction is expensive (real robots), DQN's raw sample efficiency is often inadequate without additional techniques (model-based augmentation, offline pretraining).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Deep.what_goes_wrong: DQN training is notoriously SENSITIVE to hyperparameters -- the combination of learning rate, replay buffer size, target network update frequency, exploration schedule (ε annealing), and reward scaling/clipping all interact, and a configuration that works well for one game/task often performs poorly for another with minimal changes. A common failure mode is 'Q-value explosion' -- Q-values grow to very large magnitudes (sometimes orders of magnitude beyond plausible returns) due to the overestimation bias compounding over many bootstrapped updates, eventually causing numerical instability (NaN losses) -- this is exactly the issue that Double DQN's decoupled selection/evaluation specifically mitigates, and is one reason 'plain DQN' is rarely used as-is in modern practice (Double DQN + a few other Rainbow components is closer to the practical default).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Deep.real_example: A team implements DQN for a custom discrete-action trading environment, using rewards directly proportional to dollar P&L (which can range from -$10,000 to +$10,000 per step) -- training is highly unstable, with Q-values oscillating wildly and occasionally producing NaN losses. Investigating the original DQN paper's design choices, they discover Atari DQN CLIPPED rewards to {-1, 0, +1} specifically to keep the scale of TD targets bounded and consistent across different games -- applying a similar reward NORMALIZATION (scaling P&L to a roughly [-1,1] range based on typical magnitudes) immediately stabilizes training, illustrating that DQN's published hyperparameters (including reward clipping/scaling) are often load-bearing design choices, not arbitrary details, when adapting the algorithm to a new domain.

9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Exper.what_it_is: Experience replay is a technique where the agent stores past transitions (s,a,r,s',done) in a large BUFFER (e.g. holding the last 1 million transitions), and trains the Q-network on MINI-BATCHES of transitions SAMPLED RANDOMLY from this buffer, rather than training only on the most recent transition(s) in the order they were experienced.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Exper.why_it_exists: Two problems motivate experience replay: (1) CORRELATION -- consecutive transitions from a single trajectory are highly correlated (similar states, similar actions), and training a neural network on a stream of highly-correlated data violates the i.i.d. assumption that gradient-descent-based optimization relies on, leading to inefficient or unstable learning (the network can 'overfit' to recent, correlated experience and forget about earlier, different experience -- catastrophic forgetting); (2) SAMPLE EFFICIENCY -- each environment interaction is potentially expensive (especially in real-world settings), so REUSING each transition for multiple gradient updates (by keeping it in the buffer and sampling it multiple times) extracts more learning signal per environment step than using each transition exactly once.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Exper.how_it_works: Implemented as a (typically circular/FIFO) buffer of fixed capacity -- new transitions are appended, and once full, the OLDEST transitions are overwritten. For each training step, a mini-batch of transitions is sampled UNIFORMLY AT RANDOM from the buffer (or with PRIORITY, in prioritized experience replay) -- this random sampling breaks the temporal correlation (a mini-batch contains transitions from many different points in many different trajectories, approximating i.i.d. sampling) and allows OFF-POLICY algorithms (like Q-learning/DQN) to learn from transitions generated under OLD policies (since the buffer accumulates data over potentially millions of steps, much of it generated by earlier, less-trained versions of the policy).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Exper.use_when: Experience replay is essentially MANDATORY for value-based deep RL (DQN and descendants) -- it's one of the two key stabilization techniques (alongside target networks) without which deep Q-learning is notoriously unstable. It's compatible with off-policy algorithms generally (DDPG, TD3, SAC also use replay buffers).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Exper.avoid_when: Experience replay is fundamentally an OFF-POLICY technique -- it's not directly compatible with strictly ON-POLICY algorithms (vanilla REINFORCE, A2C, PPO/TRPO in their standard forms), which require that training data come from the CURRENT policy (using stale, off-policy data from a replay buffer would bias the policy gradient estimate). PPO-style algorithms instead use a different mechanism for sample reuse (multiple epochs of minibatch updates on the SAME batch of recently-collected on-policy data, with the clipped objective limiting how far the policy can drift from the data-collecting policy within those epochs) -- this is NOT the same as a replay buffer, though it serves a loosely analogous 'reuse data for sample efficiency' purpose.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Exper.what_goes_wrong: Buffer SIZE is an important and easily-mis-set hyperparameter -- a buffer that's too SMALL means the agent effectively trains on a narrow, recent slice of experience (more correlated, less diverse -- partially defeating the purpose), while a buffer that's too LARGE means very old transitions (generated by a much-worse, early-training policy) continue to be sampled and trained on long after they're representative of current behavior, potentially slowing convergence or even pulling the policy backward toward old, worse behavior in non-stationary settings. Additionally, MEMORY consumption of large replay buffers (especially with high-dimensional observations like images) can be substantial -- a 1-million-transition buffer of 84x84x4 Atari frames at 1 byte per pixel is already ~28GB, requiring careful data-type choices (uint8 rather than float32 storage, converting only at sample time).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Exper.real_example: A team training DQN on a custom environment with image observations sets the replay buffer size to 10,000 (much smaller than the standard ~1,000,000 used for Atari), reasoning 'our environment is simpler, we don't need as much memory'. Training is unstable, with performance oscillating significantly -- investigating, they find that with their environment's episode length (~500 steps) and the small buffer, the buffer holds only about 20 episodes' worth of experience, meaning the AGENT'S RECENT (and thus highly correlated, similar-policy) EXPERIENCE DOMINATES the buffer at all times -- effectively undermining the decorrelation benefit experience replay is meant to provide. Increasing the buffer to 200,000 transitions (roughly matching the scale used for comparable published results) resolves the instability, even though their environment is indeed 'simpler' than Atari -- the relevant comparison is buffer size relative to EPISODE LENGTH and POLICY-CHANGE RATE, not absolute environment complexity.

9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Targe.what_it_is: A target network is a SECOND COPY of the Q-network's weights, θ⁻, used ONLY to compute the TD target r + γ max_{a'}Q(s',a';θ⁻) -- it's updated to match the online network θ only PERIODICALLY (e.g. every C steps, a 'hard' update: θ⁻←θ), or with a slow exponential moving average ('soft'/Polyak update: θ⁻←τθ+(1-τ)θ⁻ with small τ), rather than every gradient step.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Targe.why_it_exists: Without a target network, the TD target r + γ max_{a'}Q(s',a';θ) uses the SAME, constantly-changing parameters θ as the network being updated -- every gradient step changes θ, which changes the target for the NEXT gradient step, which is itself trying to move Q(s,a;θ) toward that (just-changed) target. This creates a feedback loop where the network is 'chasing a moving target that it itself is moving' -- analogous to a dog chasing its own tail, this can cause oscillations or divergence. Freezing the target network's parameters for a window of updates gives the online network a STABLE target to converge toward for that window, breaking this destabilizing feedback loop.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Targe.how_it_works: Two networks with identical architecture but separate weight copies: θ (online, updated every gradient step via backprop) and θ⁻ (target, used only for computing targets in the loss, NOT directly trained via gradients). Periodically (every C gradient steps, e.g. C=10,000 for Atari DQN), copy θ⁻←θ (hard update) -- so for C steps, the target network provides a fixed, stable reference, after which it 'catches up' to the online network's current state in one jump. Alternatively, SOFT updates apply θ⁻←τθ+(1-τ)θ⁻ after EVERY step with small τ (e.g. 0.005) -- giving a smoothly-lagging target rather than a step-function one (common in continuous-control algorithms like DDPG/TD3/SAC).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Targe.use_when: Target networks are used in essentially ALL value-based and actor-critic deep RL algorithms that involve bootstrapped TD targets -- DQN and descendants (hard updates, typically), DDPG/TD3/SAC (soft/Polyak updates, typically). The choice between hard and soft updates is somewhat algorithm-family-conventional (discrete-action value-based methods often use hard updates with larger C; continuous-control actor-critic methods often use soft updates with small τ), though both styles can work for either family with appropriate tuning.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Targe.avoid_when: Don't set the target update frequency/rate so AGGRESSIVELY (very small C for hard updates, or large τ for soft updates) that the target network essentially tracks the online network in real-time -- this defeats the stabilization purpose entirely, reintroducing the moving-target problem. Conversely, don't set it so CONSERVATIVELY (very large C, or tiny τ) that the target network becomes severely STALE relative to the online network's current (much-improved) policy -- an overly-stale target network means the online network is being trained toward an outdated, possibly much-worse, notion of 'optimal future value', which can slow convergence.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Targe.what_goes_wrong: The target update frequency (C, or τ) is a hyperparameter that trades off STABILITY (larger C / smaller τ → more stable, less moving-target feedback) against LAG (larger C / smaller τ → online network chases a more outdated target for longer) -- there's no universally correct value, and it often needs task-specific tuning. A common symptom of C being too LARGE (target updated too rarely) is training that's STABLE but SLOW -- the loss decreases smoothly but the policy's actual performance improves sluggishly, because the online network has 'already learned' to match a target that's many steps stale, and that stale target itself hasn't incorporated recent improvements. A symptom of C being too SMALL is the classic oscillation/instability of the moving-target problem returning.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Targe.real_example: A team training DQN observes the loss curve decreasing smoothly and consistently, suggesting 'successful training' -- but the actual game score (evaluated periodically) barely improves over the same period. Investigating, they find the target network update frequency C is set extremely high (every 50,000 steps, vs. the more typical 10,000) -- the online network IS successfully learning to match its (very stale) target, hence the smooth loss decrease, but that target reflects the policy's understanding from 50,000 steps ago, which itself hasn't incorporated much improvement yet -- the 'smooth loss decrease' was real but largely DECOUPLED from actual policy improvement. Reducing C to 10,000 produces a noisier loss curve (more frequent target shifts) but MUCH faster game-score improvement, illustrating that 'loss decreasing smoothly' isn't sufficient evidence of effective learning when the target itself can be made arbitrarily 'easy to match' by staleness.

9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Doubl.what_it_is: Double DQN modifies DQN's target computation to decouple ACTION SELECTION from ACTION EVALUATION: instead of r + γ max_{a'}Q(s',a';θ⁻) (where the target network θ⁻ both selects the best next action AND evaluates its value), Double DQN uses r + γQ(s', argmax_{a'}Q(s',a';θ); θ⁻) -- the ONLINE network θ selects which action looks best at s', while the TARGET network θ⁻ evaluates that specific action's value.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Doubl.why_it_exists: As covered in the Bellman optimality note, the max operator applied to NOISY value estimates introduces systematic OVERESTIMATION BIAS -- whichever action's estimate happens to be noisily HIGH gets selected by the max, and that same (high, possibly-overestimated) value is then used as the target. Double DQN's decoupling means that even if the ONLINE network's selection is influenced by noise (picks an action partly because its estimate is noisily high), the TARGET network's INDEPENDENT evaluation of that SAME action is less likely to share the same noise (different network weights, even if from the same architecture/training history) -- reducing (though not eliminating) the systematic overestimation.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Doubl.how_it_works: Concretely, the only change from DQN's loss is in how the bootstrapped target's 'best next action' is determined: a* = argmax_{a'}Q(s',a';θ) (using the ONLINE network's CURRENT weights -- the same network being trained), and then the target value uses Q(s',a*;θ⁻) (the TARGET network's evaluation of THAT specific action a*). This requires essentially no additional computation or architecture changes beyond DQN -- it's a one-line change in how the target is computed, reusing networks that already exist for standard DQN (online + target).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Doubl.use_when: Double DQN should essentially ALWAYS be used instead of vanilla DQN -- it's a strict, nearly-free improvement (same architecture, same computational cost, just a different target formula) that measurably reduces overestimation bias and generally improves final performance and stability. Most modern 'DQN baselines' in libraries (Stable-Baselines3, etc.) either default to Double DQN or make it a trivial flag.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Doubl.avoid_when: There's essentially no scenario where vanilla DQN's target formula is preferable to Double DQN's -- the only reason to implement vanilla DQN at all is PEDAGOGICAL (to understand the overestimation problem before seeing its fix) or for exact REPRODUCTION of historical results that used vanilla DQN.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Doubl.what_goes_wrong: A common implementation bug is getting the SELECTION/EVALUATION networks backward -- using the TARGET network for selection (argmax) and the ONLINE network for evaluation, which is the OPPOSITE of the intended decoupling and doesn't provide the same bias-reduction benefit (in fact, it can behave more like vanilla DQN with the roles of θ and θ⁻ swapped, which doesn't address the core issue since θ⁻ is the one used for the max/argmax in vanilla DQN already). Careful attention to WHICH network's parameters appear in the argmax vs. the subsequent Q-value lookup is essential -- a subtle off-by-network-reference bug that can silently reduce or eliminate Double DQN's benefit while still 'running' without errors.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Doubl.real_example: A team implements 'Double DQN' but accidentally writes `a_star = argmax_a Q(s', a; theta_target)` (using the target network for selection) followed by `target_value = Q(s', a_star; theta_online)` (using the online network for evaluation) -- the reverse of the correct formula. Training 'runs' without errors and even performs reasonably, making the bug easy to miss in casual testing. Comparing measured Q-values against empirical rollout returns (the same overestimation-bias diagnostic used for vanilla DQN) reveals the overestimation gap is nearly as large as vanilla DQN's, not reduced as Double DQN should achieve -- prompting a careful line-by-line comparison against the Double DQN paper's formula, which reveals the swapped network references.

9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Dueli.what_it_is: Dueling DQN changes the NETWORK ARCHITECTURE (not the update rule) to compute Q(s,a) as the sum of two separately-estimated streams: a STATE-VALUE stream V(s) (a single scalar, how good is this state overall) and an ADVANTAGE stream A(s,a) (one value per action, how much better/worse is THIS action compared to the average action at this state) -- combined as Q(s,a) = V(s) + (A(s,a) - mean_{a'}A(s,a')), with the mean-subtraction included for identifiability (without it, V and A could each absorb an arbitrary constant offset and still sum to the same Q, making them individually meaningless).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Dueli.why_it_exists: In MANY states, the choice of action doesn't matter much (all actions have similar Q-values, e.g. 'no enemies nearby, any movement is roughly fine') -- in such states, what matters most is V(s) (how good is this situation overall), while the RELATIVE differences between actions (A(s,a)) are small and possibly noisy to estimate precisely. Dueling DQN's architecture lets the network LEARN V(s) from EVERY action taken in state s (since V(s) is shared across all actions, every transition through s contributes to its estimate), while A(s,a) is learned more specifically per-action -- this is more SAMPLE-EFFICIENT than a standard architecture where every Q(s,a) is estimated somewhat independently, especially for large action spaces where many actions are rarely the one actually taken.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Dueli.how_it_works: The network's final layers split into two heads after a shared feature-extraction backbone: one head outputs a single scalar V(s), the other outputs a vector A(s,a) (one value per action). These are combined via Q(s,a) = V(s) + (A(s,a) - (1/|A|)Σ_{a'}A(s,a')) -- the mean-subtraction ensures that for a fixed s, A(s,a) values average to zero across actions, making V(s) interpretable as 'the expected Q-value averaged over actions' and A(s,a) as 'how much better/worse than average is action a'. This is purely an ARCHITECTURAL change -- the rest of DQN (experience replay, target network, Double-DQN-style targets) remains unchanged and Dueling DQN is typically COMBINED with Double DQN (the two improvements are orthogonal and complementary).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Dueli.use_when: Dueling DQN architecture is broadly beneficial and is a standard component of modern DQN-based agents (part of Rainbow) -- it's particularly helpful in environments with MANY actions where the relative ordering of actions doesn't change much across states (so the shared V(s) estimate captures most of the variation, and A(s,a) only needs to capture smaller refinements), but it rarely HURTS and is usually included by default in comprehensive implementations.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Dueli.avoid_when: For environments with VERY SMALL action spaces (e.g. 2 actions), the benefit of separating V(s) and A(s,a) is more marginal -- the architectural overhead (extra layers, the combination operation) provides less relative improvement when there's little 'shared structure across actions' to exploit. It's not harmful, just less impactful, for tiny action spaces.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Dueli.what_goes_wrong: A common implementation bug is forgetting the MEAN-SUBTRACTION term (using Q(s,a) = V(s)+A(s,a) directly, without subtracting mean_{a'}A(s,a')) -- without this term, the decomposition is NOT IDENTIFIABLE: the network could represent the same Q(s,a) values with infinitely many different (V,A) combinations (e.g. V(s)=10, A(s,a)=[0,1,2] gives the same Q as V(s)=12, A(s,a)=[-2,-1,0]), and during training, gradients can push V and A in directions that don't correspond to their INTENDED semantic meaning ('overall state value' vs 'relative action advantage') -- the network can still learn Q(s,a) correctly (since that's what the loss directly supervises), but the INDIVIDUAL V and A outputs become uninterpretable, which matters if you intend to USE/visualize them separately (e.g. for analysis of which states the agent considers 'high-value regardless of action').
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Dueli.real_example: A team implements Dueling DQN without the mean-subtraction term, training proceeds normally and Q(s,a) values (and resulting policy) look correct -- but when they try to VISUALIZE V(s) across the state space (expecting it to show 'overall desirability of each state', useful for understanding the agent's world-model), the V(s) values look essentially ARBITRARY/noisy, not corresponding to any sensible notion of state value. Adding the mean-subtraction term (Q=V+(A-mean(A))) doesn't change the Q-values' accuracy (training curves are nearly identical) but makes V(s) visualizations immediately sensible -- showing smoothly varying 'how good is this region of the state space' maps that match intuition, illustrating that the mean-subtraction is necessary for the DECOMPOSITION's interpretability even though it's not strictly necessary for Q(s,a) itself to be learned correctly.

9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Prior.what_it_is: Prioritized Experience Replay (PER) modifies the replay buffer to sample transitions with PROBABILITY PROPORTIONAL to their TD ERROR magnitude (|δ|) -- transitions where the network's current prediction is FAR from the TD target (large error, meaning 'the network has a lot to learn from this transition') are sampled MORE OFTEN than transitions where the prediction is already accurate (small error, 'not much new to learn here').
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Prior.why_it_exists: Uniform random sampling from the replay buffer treats all transitions equally, but transitions vary enormously in how much LEARNING SIGNAL they carry -- a transition the network already predicts accurately contributes little gradient signal, while a transition with a large TD error represents a place where the network's current estimates are notably wrong and updating on it will produce a larger, more informative gradient. PER exists to focus the LIMITED training compute on the transitions that matter most for improving the value function, analogous to how 'hard example mining' focuses supervised learning on misclassified examples.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Prior.how_it_works: Each transition in the buffer is assigned a priority p_i = |δ_i| + ε (the TD error magnitude at the time it was last sampled/computed, plus a small constant ε to ensure nonzero probability even for zero-error transitions). Sampling probability is P(i) = p_i^α / Σ_j p_j^α (α controls how strongly priority affects sampling -- α=0 is uniform, α=1 is fully proportional to priority). Because non-uniform sampling introduces BIAS (transitions are no longer sampled i.i.d. from the buffer's true distribution), PER applies IMPORTANCE SAMPLING WEIGHTS to the loss: w_i = (1/(N·P(i)))^β -- transitions sampled with HIGHER probability get DOWN-WEIGHTED in the loss, correcting for the sampling bias (β is typically annealed from a value <1 toward 1 over training, since the bias correction matters more once the policy is closer to converged). After each update, the priorities of the sampled transitions are UPDATED with their new TD errors (which will typically have decreased after the update).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Prior.use_when: PER is a standard, broadly-beneficial component of modern DQN-based agents (part of Rainbow) -- it's especially valuable in environments where 'important' transitions (e.g. those involving rare events, like a sparse reward or a critical near-failure) are RARE relative to 'routine' transitions, since uniform sampling would under-represent these important-but-rare transitions in training batches.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Prior.avoid_when: PER's implementation is more complex than uniform replay (requires a priority data structure, typically a SUM TREE for efficient O(log N) priority-proportional sampling and updates, plus importance-sampling weight bookkeeping) -- for QUICK PROTOTYPING or environments where uniform replay already performs adequately, the added implementation complexity and computational overhead (priority updates after every batch) may not be worth it, especially early in a project when iterating on other design choices is higher priority.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Prior.what_goes_wrong: A subtle issue is PRIORITY STALENESS -- a transition's priority reflects its TD error AT THE TIME IT WAS LAST SAMPLED, but the network's weights change continuously, so a transition's priority can become OUTDATED (e.g. a transition that had high TD error when first added might now have low error after many updates elsewhere in the network that happened to also improve predictions for this transition, but its STORED priority hasn't been refreshed since it hasn't been re-sampled). This means very-low-priority transitions can get 'starved' -- almost never sampled, so their priorities (and thus sampling probabilities) never get updated/refreshed, potentially leaving some transitions permanently under-trained even if they'd now have informative errors. The ε term in priority computation (ensuring nonzero sampling probability for everything) partially mitigates this but doesn't eliminate it.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Prior.real_example: A team implements PER for a sparse-reward navigation task and finds that, despite PER, the agent still struggles to learn from the (rare) goal-reaching transitions -- investigating, they find that goal-reaching transitions, when FIRST added to the buffer, have very high TD error (large priority, get sampled often initially) -- but after a burst of updates on these transitions, their TD error drops quickly (the network rapidly memorizes these specific, rare transitions), and their priority drops correspondingly, causing them to be sampled much less often going forward, even though the network's GENERALIZATION to similar-but-not-identical states near the goal is still poor. This is a known PER subtlety -- priority reflects 'error on THIS EXACT transition', not 'how much the broader value-function landscape around this transition still needs refinement' -- addressed in practice by combining PER with other techniques (e.g. Hindsight Experience Replay for sparse goal-reaching tasks specifically) rather than relying on PER alone.

9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Multi.what_it_is: This note covers n-step returns specifically as ONE OF THE RAINBOW COMPONENTS integrated into the DQN target computation -- distinct from the earlier general 'n-step returns' note (which covered the underlying TD-theory bias-variance trade-off and the off-policy/replay-buffer subtleties). Here, the focus is on the PRACTICAL INTEGRATION: replacing DQN's 1-step target r + γ max_{a'}Q(s',a';θ⁻) with an n-step target Σ_{k=0}^{n-1}γ^k r_{t+k} + γ^n max_{a'}Q(s_{t+n},a';θ⁻) (or its Double-DQN variant), and how this interacts with the other Rainbow components.
