9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Multi.why_it_exists: Within the Rainbow ablation studies, n-step returns (typically n=3) were found to be one of the most consistently impactful individual components -- providing a faster, more direct reward-propagation signal that complements the other improvements (Double DQN addresses overestimation, Dueling addresses architecture, PER addresses sampling, n-step addresses how FAR target information reaches per update). The combination matters: n-step returns reduce the NUMBER OF BOOTSTRAP STEPS needed for a reward to influence a distant state's Q-value, which is especially valuable for Atari-style games where rewards can be meaningfully delayed from the actions that caused them.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Multi.how_it_works: When sampling a transition for training, instead of using only (s_t,a_t,r_{t+1},s_{t+1}), the buffer stores/reconstructs an n-step sequence: the actual rewards r_{t+1}...r_{t+n} (collected under whatever policy was active at the time, an off-policy consideration) plus the state s_{t+n} for bootstrapping. The target becomes Σ_{k=0}^{n-1}γ^k r_{t+k+1} + γ^n Q(s_{t+n}, argmax_{a'}Q(s_{t+n},a';θ); θ⁻) (combining n-step returns with Double DQN's decoupled selection/evaluation). Implementation typically uses a small FIFO queue per ongoing trajectory to accumulate n consecutive transitions before pushing the n-step transition into the main replay buffer.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Multi.use_when: n is typically chosen in the 3-5 range for Rainbow-style DQN agents -- this is a 'sweet spot' that's been empirically validated across many Atari-like benchmarks, providing meaningfully faster reward propagation without excessive off-policy bias from mixing too many old-policy rewards into each target.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Multi.avoid_when: Don't push n much higher (e.g. n=20+) in a replay-buffer-based DQN setting -- the off-policy bias from mixing increasingly many old-policy-generated rewards into the n-step sum grows with n, and at some point this bias can outweigh the benefit of faster reward propagation, particularly in environments where the policy changes rapidly during training (so 'old' rewards in the n-step window were generated under a meaningfully different policy than the current one).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Multi.what_goes_wrong: Beyond the episode-boundary truncation issue (covered in the general n-step note), a Rainbow-specific subtlety is that n-step returns INTERACT with PRIORITIZED EXPERIENCE REPLAY's priority computation -- the TD error used for priority is now based on the n-step target, which has different statistical properties (lower bias from bootstrapping, but the n actual rewards introduce more variance) than a 1-step TD error -- a PER implementation that was tuned (e.g. its ε and α hyperparameters) assuming 1-step TD error magnitudes may need re-tuning when switching to n-step targets, since the typical MAGNITUDE of TD errors can shift.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Multi.real_example: A team adds n-step returns (n=3) to their existing DQN+Double+Dueling+PER implementation and finds PER's priority-based sampling becomes less effective -- nearly all transitions now have moderately large TD errors (since 3-step targets are noisier/less-converged than 1-step targets were), so the priority DISTRIBUTION becomes flatter, and PER's sampling looks closer to uniform than before, reducing its benefit. Re-tuning PER's α (priority exponent) slightly downward (since the underlying error distribution changed) restores a useful prioritization signal -- illustrating that Rainbow's components, while individually beneficial, can shift each other's effective hyperparameters when combined, and re-tuning after adding a new component is often necessary.

9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Distr.what_it_is: Distributional RL changes WHAT the network predicts: instead of a single scalar Q(s,a) (the EXPECTED return), the network predicts the full PROBABILITY DISTRIBUTION over possible returns Z(s,a), from which Q(s,a)=E[Z(s,a)] can be recovered as the mean -- C51 (the original distributional DQN) represents this distribution as a categorical distribution over 51 fixed 'atoms' (support values spanning the expected range of returns), while QR-DQN uses quantile regression to represent the distribution via learned quantiles instead of fixed atoms.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Distr.why_it_exists: Two returns can have the SAME expected value but very different RISK PROFILES -- e.g. an action that always yields exactly 10, vs. an action that yields 20 or 0 with equal probability, both have E[return]=10 but very different variance. A scalar Q-value can't distinguish these, but a full DISTRIBUTION can -- distributional RL was motivated partly by this richer representation enabling risk-aware decision-making, but EMPIRICALLY its main benefit turned out to be that learning the FULL DISTRIBUTION (a richer, denser training signal -- the network must get the whole shape right, not just the mean) acts as a powerful AUXILIARY/regularizing objective that improves representation learning and overall performance, even when the final POLICY still just acts on the mean (risk-neutral).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Distr.how_it_works: C51 discretizes the possible return range [V_min, V_max] into 51 equally-spaced 'atoms' z_i, and the network outputs a probability p_i(s,a) for each atom -- so Z(s,a) is represented as Σ_i p_i(s,a)δ_{z_i} (a categorical distribution over the atoms). The Bellman update for distributions involves a PROJECTION step: the target distribution r+γZ(s',a') has support shifted/scaled (by r and γ) relative to the original atoms, requiring redistribution of probability mass onto the nearest original atoms (the 'C51 projection') before computing a cross-entropy loss between the predicted and target categorical distributions. QR-DQN avoids the fixed-atom/projection complexity by instead predicting a fixed NUMBER of QUANTILES (e.g. 200 quantile VALUES, rather than probabilities over fixed values), trained via quantile regression loss -- often considered simpler to implement and tune than C51's projection step.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Distr.use_when: Distributional RL components (C51, QR-DQN, or the IQN further refinement) are part of Rainbow and broadly improve performance on standard benchmarks -- they're a good addition when you have the implementation budget for the additional complexity (especially C51's projection step, or QR-DQN's quantile regression loss) and want to extract more performance from a value-based agent. They're ESSENTIAL when the application genuinely needs RISK-SENSITIVE decision-making (e.g. preferring lower-variance returns even at the cost of slightly lower expected value, in safety-critical or financial applications) since the distribution provides the information needed for risk-aware action selection (though most implementations still act greedily on the mean unless explicitly modified for risk-sensitivity).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Distr.avoid_when: For quick prototyping or environments where the standard (scalar Q) DQN variants already perform adequately, distributional RL's added implementation complexity (especially C51's atom/projection machinery) may not be justified -- QR-DQN is a somewhat gentler entry point if you want to explore distributional methods with less implementation overhead than C51.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Distr.what_goes_wrong: For C51, the choice of V_min and V_max (the support range of the 51 atoms) is a CRITICAL hyperparameter -- if the actual range of possible returns in your environment exceeds [V_min, V_max], the projection step CLIPS target probability mass to the boundary atoms, systematically distorting the learned distribution for any returns outside the assumed range (the network literally cannot represent return values outside [V_min,V_max], no matter how the rest of training proceeds). This is a common, environment-specific tuning requirement that doesn't exist for scalar-Q methods (which have no such fixed range) -- porting C51 hyperparameters from one environment (e.g. Atari, where returns are in a roughly known range after reward clipping) to a new environment with different reward scales requires re-deriving an appropriate [V_min,V_max].
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Distr.real_example: A team adapts a C51 implementation (originally tuned for Atari with V_min=-10, V_max=10, matching clipped-reward-scale returns) to a new environment with UNCLIPPED rewards where episode returns can reach ±200 -- without updating V_min/V_max, the learned return distributions are entirely clipped to the boundary atoms (-10 and +10), and the resulting Q-value estimates (means of these clipped distributions) are wildly inaccurate for any state with a true value outside ±10. Updating V_min=-250, V_max=250 (with appropriate margin) to match the new environment's actual return range fixes the issue -- a reminder that C51's atom range is a domain-specific hyperparameter requiring re-tuning for each new task's reward scale, unlike scalar-Q methods.

9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Rainb.what_it_is: Rainbow (Hessel et al., 2017) is a single deep RL agent that combines SIX independently-developed improvements to DQN into one architecture: Double DQN (decoupled selection/evaluation), Prioritized Experience Replay, Dueling network architecture, Multi-step (n-step) returns, Distributional RL (C51), and NoisyNets (learned, state-dependent exploration noise replacing ε-greedy) -- demonstrating that these improvements are largely COMPLEMENTARY and combine to substantially outperform any single improvement alone.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Rainb.why_it_exists: Before Rainbow, each of these six improvements had been proposed and validated INDEPENDENTLY (often on slightly different benchmark subsets, with different baseline configurations), leaving open the question of whether they'd combine ADDITIVELY, REDUNDANTLY (some improvements making others unnecessary), or even CONFLICT with each other. Rainbow's systematic ablation study (training the full combination, then removing one component at a time) provided the first clear evidence of which components contribute most, and confirmed that the full combination achieves substantially better sample efficiency and final performance than any individual component or the original DQN.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Rainb.how_it_works: Architecturally, Rainbow is 'just DQN' with all six modifications applied simultaneously: the network has a DUELING architecture (separate V and A streams) with a DISTRIBUTIONAL output (C51's categorical distribution per action, per stream), trained using DOUBLE-DQN-style targets computed over N-STEP returns, sampled from a PRIORITIZED replay buffer, with NOISYNETS layers (which add learned, parametric noise to weights, providing exploration that adapts per-state/layer rather than the uniform random exploration of ε-greedy) replacing the usual ε-greedy exploration entirely. The ABLATION STUDY in the original paper is as important as the combination itself -- it ranks the components by impact (PER and multi-step returns were found to be among the most consistently important; Dueling and Distributional contributed but with somewhat smaller/more variable effect; NoisyNets had the smallest measured impact in their ablations, though this can be domain-dependent).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Rainb.use_when: Rainbow (or a close variant -- many practical implementations use a 'Rainbow-lite' with a subset of components, e.g. Double+Dueling+PER+n-step without the full distributional/NoisyNets complexity) represents the practical STATE OF THE ART for value-based, discrete-action deep RL, and is a strong default choice when discrete-action DQN-family methods are appropriate for the problem.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Rainb.avoid_when: Rainbow's full combination is COMPLEX to implement and tune correctly (six interacting components, each with its own hyperparameters) -- for early prototyping, or for problems where a simpler Double DQN + Dueling + PER baseline already performs adequately, the additional complexity of distributional RL and NoisyNets may not be worth the implementation/debugging cost. Also, Rainbow is specifically for DISCRETE action spaces -- for continuous control, the relevant 'combination of best practices' is found in SAC/TD3 rather than Rainbow.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Rainb.what_goes_wrong: Because Rainbow combines six components, DEBUGGING a Rainbow implementation that underperforms is significantly harder than debugging vanilla DQN -- a bug in any ONE component's implementation can be masked or amplified by the others, and isolating WHICH component is responsible for unexpected behavior typically requires an ABLATION approach similar to the original paper (disable components one at a time and compare). Teams implementing Rainbow from scratch (rather than using a validated library implementation) often underestimate this debugging complexity -- a subtle bug in, say, the C51 projection interacting with n-step returns' modified reward sums can produce a model that 'trains' (loss decreases) but performs poorly, with the root cause requiring systematic component-by-component isolation to find.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Value-Based Methods|Rainb.real_example: A team implements Rainbow from scratch and finds it underperforms a much simpler Double DQN + PER baseline on their environment -- rather than debugging the full six-component system directly, they follow the paper's ablation methodology: starting from their full Rainbow implementation, they disable one component at a time (e.g. first revert to ε-greedy instead of NoisyNets, then revert n-step to 1-step, etc.) and re-run short training trials after each change. They discover that disabling the DISTRIBUTIONAL (C51) component causes a large performance JUMP (toward the simpler baseline's performance) -- pointing to a bug specifically in their C51 projection step (eventually traced to an off-by-one in atom-index computation during projection). This systematic, ablation-based debugging approach -- directly mirroring how Rainbow's components were validated in the first place -- is the standard way to isolate bugs in multi-component RL systems.

9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|P.what_it_is: The policy gradient theorem provides a formula for the gradient of the expected return J(θ) (where θ are the parameters of a PARAMETERIZED, typically stochastic, policy π_θ) with respect to θ: ∇J(θ) = E_{s~d^π, a~π_θ}[∇_θ log π_θ(a|s) · Q^π(s,a)] -- this remarkable result says the gradient can be computed WITHOUT needing to differentiate through the environment's dynamics (which are typically unknown/non-differentiable), only through the POLICY itself.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|P.why_it_exists: Value-based methods (Q-learning, DQN) learn Q(s,a) and derive a policy implicitly (argmax). An alternative approach is to DIRECTLY parameterize and optimize the policy π_θ(a|s) via gradient ascent on the expected return J(θ)=E[G_0]. The challenge is that J(θ) depends on θ through a complicated chain: θ affects action probabilities, which affect the trajectory distribution, which affects the return -- and the ENVIRONMENT's transition dynamics (part of this chain) are typically unknown and non-differentiable. The policy gradient theorem is the key mathematical result showing that, remarkably, this gradient can be expressed as an expectation involving only ∇log π_θ (the score function of the policy, fully known/differentiable since you control the policy's functional form) and Q^π (the action-value, which doesn't need to be differentiated) -- the environment's dynamics appear only inside the EXPECTATION (as the distribution being sampled from), not in any derivative.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|P.how_it_works: The derivation relies on the 'log-derivative trick': ∇_θ π_θ(a|s) = π_θ(a|s)·∇_θ log π_θ(a|s) -- this lets you rewrite a gradient of a probability as that probability times a gradient of a LOG-probability, which is exactly the form needed to turn a sum/integral over actions weighted by ∇π into an EXPECTATION (sum/integral weighted by π itself, times ∇logπ) -- expectations can be ESTIMATED BY SAMPLING (Monte Carlo), which is what makes the whole approach practical: you don't need to know the environment's dynamics analytically, you just need to be able to SAMPLE trajectories from it (interact with it) and observe Q(s,a) (or an estimate thereof) for the sampled (s,a) pairs.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|P.use_when: This theorem is the foundation for EVERY policy gradient method -- REINFORCE, A2C/A3C, TRPO, PPO all derive from this same formula, differing primarily in (a) how Q^π(s,a) is estimated/approximated (Monte Carlo returns for REINFORCE, a learned critic for actor-critic methods, GAE for PPO), and (b) what additional constraints/objectives are layered on top (trust regions for TRPO, clipping for PPO). Understanding this theorem deeply is foundational for understanding WHY all these different algorithms share the same basic gradient-ascent-on-log-probability structure.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|P.avoid_when: This is foundational theory underlying an entire algorithm family, not something to 'avoid' -- but it's important not to conflate the THEOREM (an exact mathematical identity for the TRUE gradient, given the TRUE Q^π and TRUE state distribution d^π) with any PRACTICAL ALGORITHM's gradient ESTIMATE, which uses finite samples and approximate Q (introducing both variance and, for non-Monte-Carlo Q estimates, bias) -- the theorem guarantees the FORM of an unbiased gradient estimator exists; it doesn't guarantee that any particular practical implementation achieves low variance or that approximations to Q^π don't introduce additional bias.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|P.what_goes_wrong: A common point of confusion when implementing policy gradients from scratch is the SIGN and the GRADIENT DIRECTION -- since we want to MAXIMIZE J(θ) (expected return) but most deep learning frameworks default to MINIMIZING a loss via gradient DESCENT, the 'policy gradient LOSS' is typically defined as the NEGATIVE of the policy gradient objective: loss = -E[log π_θ(a|s)·Q(s,a)] (or its sample-based estimate), so that minimizing this loss corresponds to ASCENDING the true objective J(θ). Getting this sign wrong (or inconsistently applying it across the policy term vs. an entropy bonus term, which has the OPPOSITE sign convention since you want to MAXIMIZE entropy) is one of the most common 'silent' bugs in from-scratch policy gradient implementations -- the algorithm runs and 'trains' (loss decreases) but the policy gets WORSE over time, exactly the opposite of intended, because the sign error makes the optimizer DESCEND the true objective.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|P.real_example: A student implements REINFORCE from scratch and observes the policy's average return DECREASING over training, opposite to expectations -- after extensive debugging of the return computation (which is correct), they discover the loss is defined as `loss = (log_prob * G).mean()` and the optimizer performs `loss.backward(); optimizer.step()` for GRADIENT DESCENT (minimizing loss) -- but minimizing E[logπ·G] is the WRONG direction; they need to MAXIMIZE E[logπ·G], i.e. MINIMIZE its negative. Changing the loss to `loss = -(log_prob * G).mean()` immediately fixes the training direction -- the policy's average return now increases as expected. This sign convention (loss = -objective, for gradient-descent optimizers) is a near-universal gotcha in from-scratch policy gradient implementations.

9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|R.what_it_is: REINFORCE is the simplest practical instantiation of the policy gradient theorem: it estimates Q^π(s,a) using the ACTUAL MONTE CARLO RETURN G_t observed from a sampled trajectory (no separate value function/critic), giving the gradient estimate ∇J(θ) ≈ (1/N)Σ_i Σ_t ∇_θ log π_θ(a_t^{(i)}|s_t^{(i)})·G_t^{(i)}, averaged over N sampled trajectories.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|R.why_it_exists: REINFORCE is the most direct, 'textbook' application of the policy gradient theorem -- it requires NOTHING beyond the ability to sample trajectories and compute returns (no learned value function, no model) -- making it the conceptually simplest entry point into policy gradient methods, and a useful PEDAGOGICAL baseline for understanding the high-variance problem that subsequent methods (baselines, actor-critic, GAE) all address.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|R.how_it_works: For each sampled trajectory (s_0,a_0,r_1,...,s_T), compute G_t for each t (the Monte Carlo return from t to the end, as in the MDP Fundamentals note), then accumulate the gradient Σ_t ∇_θ log π_θ(a_t|s_t)·G_t -- intuitively, this INCREASES the probability of actions that were followed by HIGH returns and DECREASES the probability of actions followed by LOW (or negative) returns, weighted by HOW MUCH the return was. Because G_t is the ACTUAL observed return (not an estimate from a value function), the gradient estimate is UNBIASED -- but G_t is also a sum of many random rewards across a potentially-long trajectory, giving it HIGH VARIANCE, which translates directly into high-variance (noisy) gradient estimates.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|R.use_when: REINFORCE is rarely used as-is in modern practice -- it's primarily a TEACHING tool for understanding the policy gradient theorem's most direct form, and a useful 'simplest possible baseline' when implementing a new policy-gradient codebase from scratch (get REINFORCE working first, as a sanity check, before adding baselines/actor-critic complexity). It can be a reasonable choice for VERY SHORT-HORIZON problems where G_t's variance is manageable.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|R.avoid_when: For any problem with non-trivial episode length, REINFORCE's variance is typically TOO HIGH for efficient learning -- the gradient estimate from a single trajectory can vary enormously (since G_t depends on the entire remaining trajectory's randomness), requiring either VERY LARGE batches of trajectories per update (expensive) or VERY SMALL learning rates (slow) to avoid destabilizing the policy. Adding a BASELINE (covered next) is essentially always beneficial and is the first, simplest improvement over vanilla REINFORCE.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|R.what_goes_wrong: Without a baseline, REINFORCE's gradient updates are sensitive to the ABSOLUTE SCALE and SIGN of returns -- if all returns G_t happen to be POSITIVE (common in tasks with only positive rewards, e.g. +1 per step survived), EVERY action taken gets its probability INCREASED (since the gradient term ∇logπ·G_t is positive for all sampled (s,a,G_t)), with the RELATIVE magnitude of G_t determining how much MORE one action's probability increases vs. another's -- this can still work (relative reinforcement matters), but it means the absolute reward SCALE (e.g. +1 per step vs +100 per step) affects the EFFECTIVE LEARNING RATE in a way that's easy to overlook, since larger G_t magnitudes produce proportionally larger gradient steps for the SAME relative learning signal.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|R.real_example: A student implements REINFORCE for CartPole (reward = +1 per step survived, episodes up to 500 steps) -- with no baseline, G_t for early timesteps in long episodes can be ~50-100+ (sum of many +1's, discounted), while G_t for timesteps near the end of short (failed) episodes might be ~1-5. The gradient updates are dominated by the LONG episodes' large G_t values, even though (in an ABSOLUTE sense) every individual (s,a) pair just contributed 'the episode continued for one more step' -- the algorithm still learns (longer episodes get reinforced more, which is directionally correct), but learning is slow and sensitive to the learning rate because of this scale issue. Subtracting a baseline (e.g. the AVERAGE return across the batch, or a learned V(s)) centers the G_t values around zero, removing this scale-dependence and substantially speeding up and stabilizing training -- directly motivating the next topic.

9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|B.what_it_is: A baseline b(s) is a term subtracted from the return/Q-value in the policy gradient estimate: ∇J(θ) ≈ E[∇_θ log π_θ(a|s)·(G_t - b(s))] -- subtracting ANY function of state s alone (not depending on the action a) leaves the gradient ESTIMATE UNBIASED (this is a mathematical fact: E_a[∇logπ_θ(a|s)·b(s)] = b(s)·E_a[∇logπ_θ(a|s)] = b(s)·∇_θ(Σ_a π_θ(a|s)) = b(s)·∇_θ(1) = 0, since probabilities sum to 1), while typically REDUCING VARIANCE substantially when b(s) is chosen close to E[G_t|s_t=s] = V^π(s).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|B.why_it_exists: REINFORCE's raw G_t has high variance partly because it includes the 'baseline level of return achievable from state s regardless of action' as part of every term -- e.g. if V^π(s)≈50 for some state (any reasonable action from here yields ~50 return), then G_t values around 50 for actions from this state carry little information about WHICH ACTION was better; what matters is the DEVIATION from 50. Subtracting a baseline b(s)≈V^π(s) centers the learning signal around zero, so the gradient reflects 'was THIS action better or worse than typical for this state', which is both lower-variance and more directly the relevant comparison for improving the policy.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|B.how_it_works: The most common baseline is the LEARNED STATE-VALUE FUNCTION V_φ(s) (a separate small network, or shared-backbone output, trained via supervised regression toward observed returns: minimize (V_φ(s_t)-G_t)²). The policy gradient becomes ∇J(θ)≈E[∇logπ_θ(a|s)·(G_t-V_φ(s))] -- the term (G_t-V_φ(s)) is an ESTIMATE OF THE ADVANTAGE A(s,a)=Q(s,a)-V(s) (covered next), since G_t is a sample of Q(s,a) (the return given THIS action was taken) and V_φ(s) estimates the average over actions. This is the conceptual bridge from REINFORCE to ACTOR-CRITIC methods: once you have a learned V_φ(s) as a baseline, you've already introduced the 'critic' -- actor-critic methods just additionally use V_φ to BOOTSTRAP the return estimate itself (not just as a baseline), further reducing variance at the cost of some bias.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|B.use_when: A learned value-function baseline should be considered essentially MANDATORY for any non-trivial policy gradient method -- the variance reduction is substantial and the cost (training one additional, usually small, network) is modest. Virtually every modern policy gradient algorithm (A2C, PPO, TRPO) includes a learned baseline/critic.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|B.avoid_when: There's essentially no scenario where a state-dependent baseline HURTS (it's provably unbiased and typically reduces variance) -- the only 'cost' is the modest additional compute/implementation for training V_φ(s). One subtlety: the baseline must depend ONLY on state (not action) for the unbiasedness proof to hold -- using a baseline that depends on the ACTION TAKEN (e.g. accidentally using Q(s,a) itself as 'the baseline' rather than V(s)) would introduce BIAS, since the zero-expectation argument relies on Σ_a π(a|s)=1 being independent of which a is plugged into b.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|B.what_goes_wrong: A common implementation detail that affects results is whether the value-function baseline V_φ is trained using the SAME data/timing as the policy update, or with separate timing/learning rates -- if V_φ lags significantly behind the current policy's true V^π (e.g. trained with a much smaller learning rate, or on stale data), the baseline becomes a poor estimate of the CURRENT policy's V^π, and (G_t-V_φ(s)) no longer accurately approximates the advantage -- it can retain a systematic offset (if V_φ is uniformly too low or too high), which doesn't bias the gradient in expectation (the unbiasedness proof holds for ANY b(s), even a bad one) but DOES reduce the VARIANCE-REDUCTION BENEFIT, since the whole point of choosing b(s)≈V^π(s) was to make (G_t-b(s)) small/centered -- a poorly-fit baseline gives back some of the variance that a good baseline would have removed.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|B.real_example: A team implements actor-critic with separate learning rates for the actor (policy) and critic (value baseline), and initially sets the critic's learning rate too LOW relative to the actor's -- the critic V_φ(s) lags noticeably behind the rapidly-changing policy's true V^π(s) (especially early in training, when the policy improves quickly). The advantage estimates (G_t-V_φ(s)) remain systematically POSITIVE on average (since V_φ underestimates the now-better policy's true value), and while this doesn't bias the gradient direction catastrophically, the VARIANCE of the advantage estimates is higher than it would be with a well-fit critic -- training is noticeably less stable than expected for an actor-critic method. Increasing the critic's learning rate (so it tracks the policy's value more closely) reduces this systematic offset and the resulting training curves become smoother.

9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.what_it_is: The advantage function A^π(s,a) = Q^π(s,a) - V^π(s) measures how much BETTER (or worse) taking action a in state s is, COMPARED TO the policy's AVERAGE behaviour from s -- A>0 means a is better than average, A<0 means worse than average, and A=0 means a is exactly as good as the policy's typical action.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.why_it_exists: Raw Q(s,a) values mix together two pieces of information: 'how good is state s in general' (which is V(s), independent of a) and 'how much better/worse is THIS action relative to others from s' (which is the part that's actually USEFUL for deciding whether to increase or decrease π(a|s)). The advantage function ISOLATES the second piece -- it's exactly the quantity that appears when you subtract a V(s) baseline from Q(s,a) (as in the Baseline note), so policy gradient methods that use advantages (A2C, PPO, etc.) are directly using THIS quantity as their per-action learning signal, with the V(s) component already removed.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.how_it_works: A(s,a) can be estimated several ways: (1) Monte Carlo: A(s,a)≈G_t-V_φ(s_t) (as in the baseline note); (2) one-step TD/bootstrapped: A(s,a)≈r+γV(s')-V(s) (the TD error δ, which is itself an unbiased-in-expectation estimate of A under the TRUE V, used in A2C); (3) Generalised Advantage Estimation (GAE, covered next), which interpolates between these extremes using a λ parameter, trading bias for variance similar to TD(λ). In ALL cases, the policy gradient becomes ∇J(θ)≈E[∇logπ_θ(a|s)·A(s,a)] -- replacing Q(s,a) in the original policy gradient theorem with the advantage A(s,a), which has the SAME expected gradient direction (since the V(s) part contributes zero, as shown in the Baseline note) but LOWER VARIANCE.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.use_when: The advantage function is the standard 'currency' of modern policy gradient methods -- A2C, A3C, TRPO, PPO, and GAE all operate on advantage ESTIMATES rather than raw Q or G values. Understanding A(s,a) as 'how much better than typical' is essential for interpreting what these algorithms' loss functions are actually optimizing.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.avoid_when: A(s,a) itself isn't something to avoid -- it's a theoretical quantity. The practical question is always about the ESTIMATOR used for A(s,a) (Monte Carlo vs one-step TD vs GAE), each with different bias-variance tradeoffs as discussed in the relevant notes -- choosing the wrong estimator (e.g. pure one-step TD advantage estimates with a poorly-trained V(s), giving high bias) for a given problem is the practical concern, not the advantage function concept itself.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.what_goes_wrong: A subtle issue: A(s,a) is defined relative to the CURRENT policy π (since both Q^π and V^π depend on π) -- as the policy changes during training, the 'meaning' of A(s,a) shifts (what counted as 'better than average' under the OLD policy may not hold under the NEW policy). This is generally fine for ON-POLICY methods (A2C, PPO) that re-estimate advantages from FRESH rollouts under the current policy each update -- but it becomes a problem if advantage estimates from STALE data (collected under an old policy) are reused for many updates without re-estimation, since the advantages no longer accurately reflect 'better than average UNDER THE CURRENT POLICY'.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.real_example: In A2C, after collecting a batch of on-policy rollouts, the advantage A(s_t,a_t)≈r_t+γV_φ(s_{t+1})-V_φ(s_t) is computed using the CURRENT V_φ -- if a team mistakenly reuses these advantage estimates for MULTIPLE gradient steps (e.g. 4 epochs over the same batch, as PPO does, but without PPO's clipping safeguard), the policy can shift significantly after the first update while the advantage estimates (computed under the OLD policy/V_φ) remain fixed -- the policy gradient steps 2-4 are now optimizing against a STALE advantage signal that no longer reflects 'better than average under the NOW-CURRENT policy', leading to overly aggressive, potentially destabilizing updates. PPO's clipped objective (covered later) is specifically designed to make multi-epoch reuse of a batch SAFE despite this staleness.

9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.what_it_is: Actor-Critic is the general architecture combining TWO learned components: the ACTOR (the policy π_θ(a|s), which selects actions) and the CRITIC (the value function V_φ(s) or Q_φ(s,a), which evaluates the actor's choices) -- the critic's output (typically an advantage estimate) provides the learning signal that updates the actor via the policy gradient theorem, while the critic itself is updated via standard value-function learning (TD or Monte Carlo regression).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.why_it_exists: REINFORCE-with-baseline already has TWO learned pieces (the policy and the value-baseline), but the baseline is used purely to REDUCE VARIANCE of a Monte-Carlo return-based update -- Actor-Critic goes further by using the critic to BOOTSTRAP the return estimate ITSELF (e.g. one-step TD target r+γV(s') instead of waiting for the full Monte Carlo return G_t), enabling ONLINE, INCREMENTAL updates after every step (or short n-step segment) rather than waiting for full episodes to end -- crucial for continuing tasks (no natural episode end) and for reducing the variance/latency of learning signals in long-horizon tasks.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.how_it_works: At each step (or batch of steps): the CRITIC is updated by minimizing a TD-error-based loss (e.g. (r+γV_φ(s')-V_φ(s))² for a one-step critic), and the ACTOR is updated via ∇_θ log π_θ(a|s)·A(s,a), where A(s,a) is computed using the critic's current value estimates (e.g. A(s,a)≈r+γV_φ(s')-V_φ(s), the TD error). The two networks (or two heads of a shared network) are trained SIMULTANEOUSLY, each step improving both 'how good is this state' (critic) and 'which actions are better than average from this state' (actor) -- a continual mutual bootstrapping where a better critic gives better advantage estimates for the actor, and a better actor changes the state-visitation distribution the critic is evaluated on.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.use_when: Actor-Critic is the FOUNDATION for almost all modern deep RL policy methods -- A2C/A3C, PPO, TRPO, DDPG, TD3, SAC are all actor-critic architectures (differing in policy type -- discrete/continuous, stochastic/deterministic -- and in the specific objectives/regularizers used). Use actor-critic whenever you need a policy-gradient method with LOWER VARIANCE and ONLINE updates compared to pure Monte-Carlo REINFORCE.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.avoid_when: The bootstrapped critic introduces BIAS (the one-step TD target r+γV_φ(s') is only correct if V_φ is the TRUE value function, which it never exactly is during training) -- for problems where this bias is particularly harmful (e.g. very sparse/delayed rewards where bootstrapped estimates from an undertrained critic are wildly wrong early in training), pure Monte-Carlo methods (no bootstrapping) or longer n-step/GAE horizons (less aggressive bootstrapping) may be preferable, at the cost of higher variance.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.what_goes_wrong: A common failure mode is CRITIC COLLAPSE / DIVERGENCE feeding back into the actor -- because the actor and critic are trained SIMULTANEOUSLY and each depends on the other's output (the actor's gradient uses the critic's advantage estimate; the critic's TD target uses the CURRENT policy's behaviour, which affects the state-visitation distribution it's trained on), instabilities in one can CASCADE into the other. E.g. if the critic's value estimates become wildly inaccurate (e.g. due to a too-high learning rate causing oscillation), the advantage estimates A(s,a)=r+γV(s')-V(s) become noisy/wrong, the actor receives a bad learning signal and its policy degrades, which shifts the state distribution the critic sees, further destabilizing the critic -- a feedback loop that can cause TRAINING TO DIVERGE ENTIRELY, often abruptly after appearing to train normally for a while.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.real_example: A team training an A2C agent observes stable learning for the first ~500k steps, then a SUDDEN collapse where the policy's performance crashes to near-random within a few thousand steps and never recovers. Diagnosis: the critic's loss had been slowly INCREASING (value estimates becoming less accurate) for a while before the collapse, but this wasn't being monitored -- only the policy's episode return was tracked. Once the critic's V(s) estimates became sufficiently inaccurate, the resulting advantage signals pushed the actor toward a bad policy, which shifted the state distribution to one the critic had never seen, causing the critic's errors to compound further -- a runaway feedback loop. The fix involves monitoring BOTH actor AND critic losses/metrics (not just episode return), and often using SEPARATE, carefully-tuned learning rates (critic LR often higher than actor LR, so the critic 'keeps up' with the changing policy) plus gradient clipping on both networks.

9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.what_it_is: A2C (Advantage Actor-Critic) is a synchronous, batched implementation of the actor-critic architecture: MULTIPLE parallel environment workers each step their environment, and the resulting batch of (s,a,r,s') transitions from ALL workers is collected SYNCHRONOUSLY before a SINGLE gradient update is computed and applied to both actor and critic -- this is the 'de-asynchronized' simplification of A3C.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.why_it_exists: A3C (the original asynchronous version, covered next) used multiple CPU threads each with their OWN copy of the network parameters, updating a shared global network asynchronously -- this was effective but complex and had subtle issues (different workers could be using slightly stale/inconsistent parameter copies). A2C was introduced (notably by OpenAI) as a simpler, GPU-friendly alternative: by SYNCHRONIZING the workers (all step simultaneously, batch their results together), the algorithm can use a SINGLE set of parameters and large-batch GPU updates, achieving comparable or better performance than A3C with a simpler, more parallelizable (across GPU batch dimension) implementation.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.how_it_works: N parallel environment copies each take one step (or a short n-step rollout) using the CURRENT shared policy, producing N (or N×n) transitions -- these are batched together, advantages are computed (typically via n-step returns or simple TD: A=r+γV(s')-V(s)), and a single gradient update (combining the actor's policy-gradient loss, the critic's value loss, and often an entropy bonus for exploration) is applied to the shared network. All N workers then continue from their NEW states using the UPDATED policy for the next batch.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.use_when: A2C is a solid, simple baseline for on-policy actor-critic learning, especially when GPU parallelism across environment instances is available (e.g. vectorized environments). It's a reasonable starting point before moving to PPO (which adds clipping for more stable/sample-efficient updates) -- many codebases (e.g. Stable-Baselines3) implement both, with PPO generally recommended as the default due to its improved stability and sample efficiency from multi-epoch reuse of batches.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.avoid_when: A2C lacks PPO's trust-region-like safeguards (clipping), so large policy updates from a single batch can be destabilizing -- if training is unstable with A2C (oscillating or diverging returns), PPO's clipped objective (allowing safer multi-epoch reuse of the same batch with bounded policy change per update) is usually a direct and effective upgrade. A2C is also generally LESS sample-efficient than off-policy methods (SAC, TD3) for continuous control, since each batch of experience is used for exactly ONE gradient update and then discarded (strictly on-policy).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.what_goes_wrong: A common issue is the GRADIENT-STEP-TO-EXPERIENCE ratio being implicitly TOO LOW for sample efficiency -- since A2C performs exactly one update per batch of N×n_steps transitions (no experience reuse, strictly on-policy), increasing the NUMBER of environment steps used per update (by increasing N parallel workers or n_steps per rollout) increases SAMPLE efficiency per WALL-CLOCK time (more parallelism) but does NOT increase how many TIMES each piece of experience contributes to learning -- teams sometimes mistakenly believe 'more parallel environments = more sample-efficient learning' when it primarily means 'more environment steps consumed per unit wall-clock time', without changing the fundamental on-policy, single-use-per-sample nature of the algorithm.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.real_example: A team compares A2C with 8 parallel environments against A2C with 32 parallel environments on the same task, expecting the 32-env version to reach a target return in FEWER ENVIRONMENT STEPS (better sample efficiency) -- but observes roughly the SAME number of environment steps to convergence (just achieved in less wall-clock time due to parallelism). This is expected: A2C's sample efficiency (return per environment step) is governed by factors like learning rate, entropy bonus, and advantage estimation quality -- NOT by the degree of parallelism, which primarily affects wall-clock throughput. To IMPROVE sample efficiency (fewer total environment steps), the team would need algorithmic changes (e.g. switching to PPO for multi-epoch batch reuse, or to an off-policy method like SAC for experience replay).

9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.what_it_is: A3C (Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic) is the original parallel actor-critic algorithm (Mnih et al. 2016): MULTIPLE CPU worker threads, each with its OWN copy of the actor-critic network and its OWN environment instance, independently compute gradients from short n-step rollouts and ASYNCHRONOUSLY apply these gradients to a SHARED global network -- each worker periodically pulls the latest global parameters before continuing.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.why_it_exists: Before A3C, training deep RL agents typically required either expensive GPU-based experience replay (DQN) or was limited to a single environment instance, making wall-clock training time very slow for complex tasks. A3C showed that running MANY lightweight CPU workers, each exploring a DIFFERENT part of the environment (or different random seeds) in PARALLEL, and asynchronously contributing gradients to a shared network, could achieve fast, stable training WITHOUT a replay buffer (the diversity of experience comes from the DIFFERENT workers' different trajectories at any given moment, serving a decorrelation role similar to replay).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.how_it_works: Each worker thread: (1) copies the current global network parameters locally, (2) runs n steps (e.g. n=5-20) in its own environment instance using its local policy, (3) computes the actor-critic gradient (policy gradient + value loss + entropy bonus) from this n-step rollout using n-step returns as advantage estimates, (4) ASYNCHRONOUSLY applies this gradient to the GLOBAL shared network (via Hogwild-style lock-free updates), and (5) repeats from step 1 with the (possibly updated by other workers) global parameters. Because workers update asynchronously and use possibly slightly-stale local copies, gradients are somewhat 'noisy'/inconsistent with each other -- but in practice this acts as a mild regularizer and the diversity across workers' experience provides the decorrelation that experience replay provides for DQN.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.use_when: A3C was historically important as the first algorithm to demonstrate efficient CPU-parallel deep RL training without replay buffers, achieving strong results on Atari with far less wall-clock time than DQN. In modern practice, A3C has been largely SUPERSEDED by A2C (its synchronous, GPU-friendly variant) and PPO (which builds on the same actor-critic foundation with better stability) -- understanding A3C is mostly useful for HISTORICAL CONTEXT and for understanding the asynchronous-vs-synchronous design tradeoff in distributed RL (also relevant to IMPALA and other distributed RL systems).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.avoid_when: For new projects, A3C's asynchronous CPU-thread architecture is rarely the right choice -- A2C (synchronous, GPU-batchable) or PPO (with clipping for stability) achieve comparable or better results with simpler, more reproducible implementations. The asynchronous gradient updates in A3C also make EXACT REPRODUCIBILITY difficult (the order/timing of worker updates is non-deterministic), which is undesirable for research requiring careful comparisons.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.what_goes_wrong: The CORE risk in A3C is STALE GRADIENTS -- because each worker computes its gradient using a LOCAL COPY of parameters that may be several updates BEHIND the current global parameters (other workers may have applied updates in the meantime), the gradient being applied may not correspond to the CURRENT global parameters' loss landscape. With too many workers or too-infrequent parameter syncing, this staleness can accumulate and destabilize training -- a phenomenon sometimes called the 'stale gradient problem' in asynchronous distributed optimization, which becomes worse as the number of parallel workers increases relative to how quickly each worker syncs.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|A.real_example: In the original A3C paper, experiments showed that performance on Atari games improved with MORE parallel workers (e.g. from 1 to 16) up to a point, but the gains were SUB-LINEAR (16 workers didn't give 16x the effective learning rate) -- partly attributable to the staleness of asynchronous gradients: with more workers, each worker's local parameter copy is more likely to be stale by the time its gradient is applied. This is a key reason later work (A2C, IMPALA with V-trace correction for off-policy bias from staleness) moved toward either SYNCHRONOUS updates (A2C, eliminating staleness entirely) or EXPLICIT CORRECTIONS for the staleness/off-policy-ness introduced by asynchrony (IMPALA's V-trace).

9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|G.what_it_is: Generalised Advantage Estimation (GAE-λ, Schulman et al. 2016) is a method for estimating the advantage function A(s,a) that INTERPOLATES between high-bias/low-variance one-step TD advantage estimates (λ=0) and low-bias/high-variance Monte-Carlo advantage estimates (λ=1), using an exponentially-weighted average of n-step advantage estimates for ALL n, controlled by a single parameter λ∈[0,1].
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|G.why_it_exists: The advantage estimator choice (one-step TD δ_t=r_t+γV(s_{t+1})-V(s_t) vs full Monte-Carlo G_t-V(s_t) vs something in between) directly trades off BIAS (one-step TD is biased if V is imperfect, which it always is during training) against VARIANCE (Monte Carlo has high variance from summing many random rewards) -- this is exactly the same bias-variance spectrum as TD(λ) for value-function learning (covered in Model-Free Methods), but GAE applies the SAME exponentially-weighted multi-step idea specifically to ADVANTAGE estimation for policy gradients, providing a smooth, single-hyperparameter (λ) way to tune this tradeoff and, empirically, dramatically improving the stability and sample-efficiency of actor-critic methods like PPO and TRPO compared to using either extreme.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|G.how_it_works: Define the one-step TD error δ_t=r_t+γV(s_{t+1})-V(s_t). The n-step advantage estimate is A_t^{(n)}=Σ_{k=0}^{n-1}γ^k δ_{t+k} (sum of n one-step TD errors, which telescopes to approximately G_t^{(n)}-V(s_t)). GAE-λ defines A_t^{GAE(λ)}=(1-λ)Σ_{n=1}^∞ λ^{n-1}A_t^{(n)}, which simplifies to a simple recursive/forward computation: A_t^{GAE(λ)}=Σ_{k=0}^∞(γλ)^k δ_{t+k} -- i.e. an exponentially-decayed sum of FUTURE TD errors, with decay rate (γλ). At λ=0, this reduces to the one-step TD error δ_t (high bias if V imperfect, low variance); at λ=1, it reduces to the full Monte-Carlo advantage G_t-V(s_t) (unbiased, high variance). λ≈0.9-0.97 is a common practical sweet spot.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|G.use_when: GAE is used in virtually ALL modern on-policy actor-critic algorithms -- PPO and TRPO both use GAE (with λ typically 0.95) as their standard advantage estimator, because it substantially improves sample efficiency and training stability compared to either one-step TD or pure Monte-Carlo advantages. If implementing PPO/TRPO/A2C from scratch, GAE should be the default advantage estimator unless there's a specific reason to use something simpler.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|G.avoid_when: GAE requires the rollout to be (at least conceptually) a finite sequence ending in either episode termination or a value-function 'bootstrap' at the cutoff (V(s_T) for the last state in a truncated rollout) -- the computation is a backward recursion over the rollout, so it adds modest implementation complexity compared to a pure one-step TD advantage. For VERY SHORT rollouts (e.g. n_steps=1), GAE with any λ reduces to (approximately) the one-step TD advantage anyway, so the added complexity may not be worth it.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|G.what_goes_wrong: A common implementation bug is mishandling the BOOTSTRAP VALUE at the END of a truncated rollout (as opposed to a true episode termination) -- if a rollout is cut off mid-episode (common with fixed-length rollouts in parallel environments), the GAE computation needs V(s_T) (the critic's estimate of the value of the LAST state in the rollout, even though the episode continues beyond it) to correctly 'continue' the advantage estimate beyond the rollout boundary. If this bootstrap is mistakenly OMITTED (treating the rollout cutoff as if it were a true terminal state, i.e. using V(s_T)=0), the advantage estimates for the LAST few timesteps in each rollout become systematically BIASED (typically underestimating returns for ongoing episodes), which can subtly degrade learning, especially with long-horizon tasks and short rollout lengths.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|G.real_example: A team implementing PPO for a continuing (non-episodic) robotics task uses rollouts of length 128 steps per environment, but their GAE implementation sets the 'done' flag-equivalent bootstrap to V=0 at the END of every 128-step chunk (treating each chunk as if it were a complete episode) rather than bootstrapping with V_φ(s_128) (the critic's estimate for the actual continuing state). This systematically UNDERESTIMATES the value/advantage of states near the END of each rollout chunk (since the true future reward beyond step 128 is ignored), creating a periodic bias pattern correlated with position-within-rollout -- the agent learns a subtly distorted value function that's most inaccurate for 'late-in-rollout' states. Fixing the bootstrap to use V_φ(s_128) (the critic's own estimate) for non-terminal rollout cutoffs removes this artifact.

9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|T.what_it_is: TRPO (Schulman et al. 2015) is a policy gradient algorithm that constrains EACH policy update to stay within a 'trust region' -- a bounded KL-divergence D_KL(π_old || π_new) ≤ δ between the old and new policy -- by solving a CONSTRAINED optimization problem (maximize the surrogate advantage objective subject to the KL constraint) using conjugate gradient methods and a line search, guaranteeing MONOTONIC IMPROVEMENT (in theory) of the policy's expected return.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|T.why_it_exists: Naive policy gradient methods (REINFORCE, vanilla actor-critic) can take a gradient step that's too LARGE, causing the policy to change DRASTICALLY in one update -- because the data used to compute the gradient was collected under the OLD policy, a too-large step can move to a region where that data is no longer representative, potentially causing a CATASTROPHIC drop in performance from which the policy may never recover (since subsequent updates are based on the now-bad policy's behaviour). TRPO addresses this by EXPLICITLY BOUNDING how much the policy can change (in KL-divergence terms) per update, providing a theoretical guarantee that, under certain approximations, EVERY update improves (or at least doesn't significantly worsen) the policy.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|T.how_it_works: TRPO maximizes a 'surrogate' objective L(θ)=E[π_θ(a|s)/π_θ_old(a|s)·A^{θ_old}(s,a)] (an importance-sampling-corrected estimate of the improvement from moving to θ, evaluated using data collected under θ_old), SUBJECT TO the constraint E[D_KL(π_θ_old(·|s)||π_θ(·|s))]≤δ. This constrained optimization is solved approximately using a SECOND-ORDER method: compute the gradient of L and the Fisher Information Matrix (related to the Hessian of the KL constraint), use CONJUGATE GRADIENT to compute a search direction without explicitly forming/inverting the (huge) Fisher matrix, then perform a LINE SEARCH along this direction to find the largest step that satisfies the KL constraint AND improves L.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|T.use_when: TRPO was historically important for demonstrating that strong theoretical guarantees (monotonic improvement) could translate into PRACTICALLY more stable training than vanilla policy gradients, particularly for continuous-control tasks (robotic locomotion, etc.) where naive methods often diverged. It remains a useful CONCEPTUAL reference point for understanding 'trust region' ideas, and is sometimes still used when its theoretical guarantees are specifically valued (e.g. in safety-critical settings where monotonic-improvement-style guarantees matter).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|T.avoid_when: TRPO's conjugate-gradient + line-search machinery is SIGNIFICANTLY more complex to implement correctly than PPO's simple clipped objective, and in practice PPO achieves COMPARABLE OR BETTER performance with a small fraction of the implementation complexity (no second-order optimization, just standard SGD/Adam on a clipped objective) -- for almost all practical purposes, PPO has SUPERSEDED TRPO as the default choice, and TRPO is rarely the right pick for a new project unless its specific theoretical guarantees are required.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|T.what_goes_wrong: TRPO's conjugate-gradient step for computing the natural-gradient-like search direction requires multiple Hessian-vector-product evaluations (via the Fisher Information Matrix), which are computationally expensive -- if the conjugate-gradient iteration count is too LOW (for compute efficiency), the search direction can be a POOR APPROXIMATION to the true natural gradient direction, undermining the theoretical guarantees that motivated TRPO in the first place. There's a delicate tradeoff between computational cost (more CG iterations = more accurate direction = more expensive per update) and the quality of the trust-region approximation -- getting this wrong can result in TRPO performing WORSE than simpler methods despite its more sophisticated theory, simply because the practical approximations break the guarantees.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|T.real_example: Early TRPO implementations on continuous-control benchmarks (MuJoCo) found that the algorithm's wall-clock training time was dominated by the conjugate-gradient Hessian-vector-product computations (often 10+ CG iterations per update, each requiring a full forward+backward pass through the policy network for the Fisher-vector product) -- this made TRPO 5-10x SLOWER per update than a simple actor-critic method, despite often requiring FEWER updates to reach a given performance level due to its stability. When PPO was introduced shortly after (by the same research group), benchmarks showed PPO matching or exceeding TRPO's final performance while being dramatically faster per-update (simple first-order SGD/Adam, no CG) -- this practical speed/simplicity advantage, combined with comparable results, is the primary reason PPO became the de facto standard over TRPO.

9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|P.what_it_is: PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization, Schulman et al. 2017) is a policy gradient algorithm that achieves TRPO-like update stability using a much simpler FIRST-ORDER method: it optimizes a CLIPPED surrogate objective L^{CLIP}(θ)=E[min(r_t(θ)·A_t, clip(r_t(θ),1-ε,1+ε)·A_t)], where r_t(θ)=π_θ(a_t|s_t)/π_θ_old(a_t|s_t) is the probability ratio between new and old policies, and ε (typically 0.1-0.3) controls how far the ratio is allowed to deviate from 1 before the objective stops providing a gradient signal.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|P.why_it_exists: PPO was designed to capture TRPO's core benefit (preventing destructively large policy updates) WITHOUT TRPO's implementation complexity (conjugate gradient, Fisher-vector products, line search) -- by simply CLIPPING the objective so that the incentive to increase r_t(θ) beyond (1+ε) [or decrease beyond (1-ε)] for advantageous [or disadvantageous] actions disappears, PPO discourages the optimizer from moving the policy too far in a single update USING ONLY STANDARD SGD/ADAM, making it dramatically simpler to implement, tune, and parallelize than TRPO -- this simplicity, combined with strong empirical performance, made PPO the DEFAULT choice for on-policy RL across domains (from Atari/MuJoCo to RLHF for LLMs).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|P.how_it_works: For each minibatch of (s,a,A) from a rollout collected under π_θ_old: compute the ratio r_t(θ)=π_θ(a_t|s_t)/π_θ_old(a_t|s_t); the UNCLIPPED objective r_t(θ)·A_t would be the standard importance-sampling-corrected policy gradient surrogate -- but PPO takes the MINIMUM of this and a CLIPPED version clip(r_t(θ),1-ε,1+ε)·A_t. The min() with clipping means: for POSITIVE advantages (A_t>0, action was better than average), the objective is capped once r_t(θ)>1+ε (no further incentive to push the policy MORE toward this action beyond that ratio); for NEGATIVE advantages (A_t<0), the objective is capped once r_t(θ)<1-ε (no further incentive to push AWAY beyond that ratio). This allows MULTIPLE EPOCHS of minibatch updates over the SAME rollout batch (improving sample efficiency vs. A2C's single update per batch) while the clipping prevents any single epoch's updates from driving the policy too far from π_θ_old (where the batch's advantage estimates remain roughly valid).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|P.use_when: PPO is the DEFAULT, go-to algorithm for on-policy RL across an enormous range of applications -- robotics control, game-playing agents, and notably RLHF for fine-tuning LLMs (see Phase 5). Its combination of simplicity, stability, decent sample efficiency (via multi-epoch reuse), and robustness to hyperparameters makes it the standard 'first thing to try' for new RL problems, especially when a reasonably-parallelizable simulator/environment is available for collecting on-policy rollouts.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|P.avoid_when: PPO is still fundamentally ON-POLICY -- each batch of rollouts is used for a handful of epochs and then DISCARDED, making it less sample-efficient than OFF-POLICY methods (SAC, TD3, DQN-family) for problems where environment interaction is EXPENSIVE (e.g. real robots, where every step has physical cost) and a large replay buffer of past experience could be reused indefinitely. For such sample-efficiency-critical settings, off-policy methods are often preferred despite their additional complexity/instability risks.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|P.what_goes_wrong: A frequently-misunderstood point is that PPO's clipping does NOT prevent the policy from EVER moving the ratio r_t(θ) outside [1-ε,1+ε] -- it only removes the GRADIENT INCENTIVE to do so for THAT TERM. Across MULTIPLE epochs/updates, the policy CAN still drift the ratio outside the clip range (since the clip is recomputed each epoch relative to the ORIGINAL π_θ_old from data collection, while θ keeps changing) -- if this drift becomes large (often measured via the empirical KL divergence between π_θ_old and the current π_θ), the importance-sampling-based surrogate objective becomes increasingly INACCURATE (the batch's advantage estimates, computed under π_θ_old, are less and less representative of π_θ's behaviour). Many implementations add an EARLY STOPPING criterion: if the average KL divergence exceeds a threshold during the epoch loop, stop updating on this batch early, even if the planned number of epochs hasn't been reached.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|P.real_example: A team trains PPO with the default 4 epochs over each rollout batch and observes that on EASY tasks training is stable, but on a HARDER task with high-variance advantage estimates, training occasionally exhibits sudden performance drops after seemingly-normal updates. Diagnosis via logging the empirical KL divergence between π_θ_old and π_θ_current AFTER EACH EPOCH reveals that on the harder task, KL grows much faster across epochs (sometimes 5-10x the typical value by epoch 4) -- the clipping wasn't sufficient to prevent the AGGREGATE drift across 4 full epochs from becoming large. Adding an early-stopping rule (stop epoch loop if KL > 1.5x target_kl) for this batch resolves the sudden drops -- the policy still improves, just with fewer effective epochs on batches where the surrogate objective would otherwise become too stale/inaccurate.

9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|P.what_it_is: The entropy bonus is an additional term added to PPO's (and other policy gradient methods') loss function: L^{total}=L^{CLIP}-c_1·L^{VF}+c_2·H[π_θ(·|s)], where H[π_θ(·|s)] is the SHANNON ENTROPY of the policy's action distribution at state s, and c_2 is a (typically small, e.g. 0.0-0.01) coefficient -- since the loss is MAXIMIZED (or its negative minimized), this term REWARDS the policy for maintaining HIGHER ENTROPY (more randomness/uncertainty in its action distribution), counteracting the natural tendency of policy gradient updates to make the policy increasingly DETERMINISTIC/PEAKED over time.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|P.why_it_exists: Policy gradient updates inherently push π_θ(a|s) toward PUTTING MORE PROBABILITY MASS on actions with high advantage -- left unchecked, this can cause the policy to become PREMATURELY DETERMINISTIC (entropy →0) before it has adequately explored the action space, getting stuck in a LOCAL OPTIMUM (a suboptimal but 'good enough' behaviour that the policy becomes too confident in to deviate from). The entropy bonus provides an explicit, tunable counterforce -- a small reward for 'staying uncertain a bit longer' -- which encourages continued EXPLORATION during training, particularly important early in training when the value/advantage estimates are still unreliable and 'confidently committing' to an action based on noisy advantage estimates could be premature.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|P.how_it_works: For a discrete (categorical) policy, H[π_θ(·|s)]=-Σ_a π_θ(a|s)log π_θ(a|s) -- maximal when all actions are equally likely (uniform distribution), and zero when the policy is fully deterministic (one action has probability 1). For continuous (Gaussian) policies, the entropy is a function of the standard deviation σ -- a higher σ (more spread-out action distribution) gives higher entropy, so the entropy bonus directly discourages σ from collapsing to near-zero too quickly. The coefficient c_2 is typically annealed (decreased) over training, or kept small and fixed -- too large a value can prevent the policy from ever converging to a sufficiently confident/sharp distribution, hurting final performance, while too small (or zero) a value risks premature convergence/local optima, especially in tasks with deceptive or sparse reward landscapes.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|P.use_when: An entropy bonus is standard practice for nearly all on-policy policy gradient methods (A2C, A3C, PPO, TRPO) and is particularly important for tasks with: (a) multiple distinct strategies of similar quality (where premature commitment to one is risky), (b) sparse or deceptive rewards (where early advantage estimates are unreliable and might point toward suboptimal local optima), or (c) discrete action spaces with many actions (where the policy collapsing to a single action early can prevent discovering better alternatives).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|P.avoid_when: For tasks where a NEAR-DETERMINISTIC policy is the known optimal behaviour and exploration concerns are minimal (e.g. late-stage fine-tuning of an already-good policy, or tasks where the optimal policy genuinely IS close to deterministic), a large entropy coefficient can actively HURT final performance by preventing the policy from sharpening sufficiently -- in RLHF fine-tuning of LLMs, for instance, entropy bonuses are often kept very small or omitted, since excessive entropy can manifest as degraded/incoherent outputs.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|P.what_goes_wrong: A common issue is using a FIXED entropy coefficient that's appropriate for EARLY training but becomes too large RELATIVE TO the policy-gradient and value-loss terms LATER in training, once those terms' magnitudes have naturally decreased as the policy converges -- this can cause the policy's entropy to PLATEAU at an artificially high level (the entropy bonus 'fights' the policy gradient's natural convergence pressure to a draw), preventing the policy from ever becoming confident enough to perform optimally, manifesting as persistently noisy/suboptimal behaviour even after the value function appears to have converged.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Policy Gradient Methods|P.real_example: A team trains PPO on a navigation task and observes that episode returns plateau at a SUBOPTIMAL level -- investigation shows the policy's action-distribution entropy remains relatively HIGH throughout training (the agent continues taking noticeably random-looking actions even late in training, when a more confident/deterministic policy would perform better). The entropy coefficient c_2 was set based on early-training tuning (when the policy-gradient loss magnitude was large, so a moderate c_2 was 'balanced'), but as training progressed and the policy-gradient loss naturally shrunk (advantages became smaller as the policy approached a local optimum), the now-RELATIVELY-LARGE entropy term continued pushing for randomness, preventing further sharpening. Annealing c_2 to a smaller value over training (or using a smaller fixed value from the start) allows the policy to converge to a sharper, better-performing distribution in later training.

9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Continuous Action RL|DDPG.what_it_is: DDPG (Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient, Lillicrap et al. 2015) is an OFF-POLICY actor-critic algorithm for CONTINUOUS action spaces: the actor learns a DETERMINISTIC policy μ_θ(s)→a (directly outputs an action, not a probability distribution), and the critic Q_φ(s,a) is trained via the standard Q-learning Bellman update (like DQN) to evaluate (state, action) pairs -- the actor is updated to maximize Q_φ(s,μ_θ(s)) via the chain rule, since both μ_θ and Q_φ are differentiable.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Continuous Action RL|DDPG.why_it_exists: Policy gradient methods like REINFORCE/A2C/PPO with STOCHASTIC policies require sampling actions and computing log-probabilities, which doesn't extend cleanly to choosing the SINGLE BEST action in continuous spaces with a fully deterministic policy. Meanwhile, DQN-style Q-learning requires taking argmax_a Q(s,a) -- trivial for discrete actions (enumerate and compare) but INTRACTABLE for continuous actions (infinite possibilities, no closed-form argmax for an arbitrary neural network Q). DDPG resolves this by learning a DETERMINISTIC ACTOR μ_θ(s) that DIRECTLY APPROXIMATES argmax_a Q_φ(s,a) -- the actor IS the (learned) argmax operator, trained via gradient ascent on Q_φ(s,μ_θ(s)) using the deterministic policy gradient theorem (a special case of the policy gradient theorem for deterministic policies).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Continuous Action RL|DDPG.how_it_works: DDPG maintains FOUR networks: actor μ_θ, critic Q_φ, and their TARGET copies μ_θ', Q_φ' (updated via slow Polyak/soft averaging: θ'←τθ+(1-τ)θ', similar to DQN's target network but updated continuously rather than periodically). The critic is trained via TD: minimize (Q_φ(s,a)-(r+γQ_φ'(s',μ_θ'(s'))))² -- using the TARGET actor to select the next action (since there's no argmax to compute, just evaluate Q at the target actor's deterministic choice). The actor is trained via ∇_θ E[Q_φ(s,μ_θ(s))] = E[∇_a Q_φ(s,a)|_{a=μ_θ(s)}·∇_θ μ_θ(s)] (chain rule through Q). Off-policy EXPERIENCE REPLAY (like DQN) provides sample efficiency. Since the policy is DETERMINISTIC, EXPLORATION requires adding NOISE to actions during data collection (e.g. Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noise or simple Gaussian noise added to μ_θ(s)).
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Continuous Action RL|DDPG.use_when: DDPG was historically important as the first widely-used deep RL algorithm for continuous control with off-policy sample efficiency -- it's a useful CONCEPTUAL stepping stone to TD3 and SAC. In modern practice, DDPG itself is rarely chosen directly due to well-documented instability issues; TD3 (which directly fixes DDPG's main weaknesses) or SAC are almost always preferred.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Continuous Action RL|DDPG.avoid_when: DDPG is notoriously SENSITIVE to hyperparameters and prone to Q-VALUE OVERESTIMATION (similar to the overestimation bias in vanilla Q-learning/DQN, but exacerbated because the actor is EXPLICITLY trained to find actions that MAXIMIZE Q_φ -- if Q_φ has any systematic overestimation for certain actions, the actor will be DRAWN TOWARD exploiting exactly those overestimated regions, a feedback loop that DQN with discrete argmax doesn't suffer from as severely). For new projects, TD3 or SAC should be used instead of vanilla DDPG.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Continuous Action RL|DDPG.what_goes_wrong: The Q-VALUE OVERESTIMATION feedback loop is DDPG's signature failure mode: because the actor is trained via gradient ASCENT on Q_φ(s,μ_θ(s)), it will naturally gravitate toward regions of action-space where Q_φ happens to be OVERESTIMATED (due to function approximation error, noise in TD targets, etc.) -- and because the actor's output μ_θ(s) then BECOMES the action evaluated/trained on, the critic's TD targets increasingly involve these overestimated regions, REINFORCING the overestimation. This compounding effect can cause Q-values to DIVERGE to unrealistically large values while the actual POLICY PERFORMANCE (measured by episode return) STAGNATES OR DEGRADES -- a classic 'overoptimistic critic, useless actor' failure that's hard to diagnose without specifically comparing Q_φ's predicted values against ACTUAL observed returns.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Continuous Action RL|DDPG.real_example: A team trains DDPG on a continuous-control task and observes the critic's predicted Q-values steadily INCREASING throughout training (reaching values far larger than any plausible discounted-return given the reward scale), while the actual episode returns PLATEAU or even DECLINE after initial progress. Plotting predicted-Q vs actual-return reveals a growing gap -- the critic has learned to assign artificially high values to the actions the (increasingly confident) actor proposes, a self-reinforcing overestimation loop. Switching to TD3 (same overall architecture, but using the MINIMUM of TWO critics for the TD target, directly countering this overestimation) resolves the divergence -- predicted Q-values track actual returns much more closely, and the policy continues improving instead of stagnating.

9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Continuous Action RL|Twin.what_it_is: TD3 (Fujimoto et al. 2018) is DDPG with THREE specific modifications that directly address DDPG's overestimation and instability issues: (1) CLIPPED DOUBLE Q-LEARNING -- train TWO independent critics Q_φ1, Q_φ2 and use the MINIMUM of their target predictions for the TD target; (2) DELAYED POLICY UPDATES -- update the actor (and target networks) less frequently than the critics (e.g. every 2 critic updates); (3) TARGET POLICY SMOOTHING -- add clipped noise to the target action used in the TD target, regularizing the Q-function against sharp errors near specific actions.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Continuous Action RL|Twin.why_it_exists: Each of TD3's three tricks targets a SPECIFIC failure mode of DDPG: (1) the twin-critic minimum directly counters the Q-OVERESTIMATION feedback loop described in the DDPG note (analogous to Double DQN's decoupling, but here BOTH critics are independently trained and the MINIMUM is taken, a more conservative/pessimistic choice than Double DQN's selection-vs-evaluation decoupling); (2) delayed actor updates give the critic(s) time to become MORE ACCURATE before the actor exploits them, reducing how often the actor chases a still-noisy/inaccurate Q estimate; (3) target policy smoothing prevents the critic from learning a NARROW, SHARP peak in Q(s,a) around one specific action (which the deterministic actor could then exploit/overfit to) by forcing Q to be smooth over a small neighborhood of actions around μ_θ'(s').
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Continuous Action RL|Twin.how_it_works: Critic update: y=r+γ·min(Q_φ1'(s',ã'), Q_φ2'(s',ã')), where ã'=μ_θ'(s')+clip(ε,-c,c), ε~N(0,σ) (the target-policy-smoothing noise, clipped to a small range). BOTH Q_φ1 and Q_φ2 are trained toward this SAME (shared, minimum-based) target y. Actor update: every d critic updates (e.g. d=2), update μ_θ via ∇_θ Q_φ1(s,μ_θ(s)) (using just ONE of the critics, by convention), and softly update all target networks (μ_θ', Q_φ1', Q_φ2').
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Continuous Action RL|Twin.use_when: TD3 is a strong, relatively simple, well-tested choice for continuous-action off-policy RL, particularly for tasks where a DETERMINISTIC final policy is desired (e.g. for deployment, where you want REPRODUCIBLE behaviour rather than a stochastic policy's sampling variability). It's commonly used as a baseline in continuous-control research and robotics.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Continuous Action RL|Twin.avoid_when: TD3's deterministic policy means EXPLORATION still relies on EXTERNALLY ADDED NOISE (Gaussian noise on top of μ_θ(s) during data collection) -- this is a less PRINCIPLED exploration mechanism than SAC's entropy-regularized STOCHASTIC policy, which explores 'natively' via its action distribution and automatically reduces exploration as the policy becomes more confident. For tasks where exploration is particularly challenging (sparse rewards, complex action spaces), SAC's maximum-entropy framework is often preferred.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Continuous Action RL|Twin.what_goes_wrong: A common tuning issue is the INTERACTION between the delayed policy update frequency (d) and the soft-update rate (τ) for target networks -- if d is too LARGE relative to how quickly the environment/policy is changing, the actor can become STALE relative to the critics' current estimates, slowing learning; if d is too SMALL, TD3 degrades toward vanilla DDPG's overestimation-prone behaviour (since the actor exploits the critics' current estimates too eagerly, before they've had time to stabilize from the previous actor update). The 'sweet spot' (d=2 is the paper's default) can be sensitive to the specific environment's dynamics and reward scale.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Continuous Action RL|Twin.real_example: A team applies TD3 to a new robotic manipulation task using the paper's default hyperparameters (d=2, target smoothing noise σ=0.2, clip=0.5) but finds training significantly slower than on the benchmark MuJoCo tasks TD3 was originally tuned on -- the new task has a much SMALLER action range (e.g. joint velocities in [-0.1,0.1] rather than [-1,1]), so the FIXED noise σ=0.2 for target policy smoothing is RELATIVELY HUGE compared to the action scale, effectively making the critic's TD targets extremely noisy (smoothing over almost the entire action range) -- the critic struggles to learn meaningful Q-value differences between actions. Rescaling the smoothing noise (and exploration noise) proportionally to the task's actual action range restores TD3's expected performance, illustrating that TD3's 'tuned' hyperparameters are often IMPLICITLY CALIBRATED to specific benchmark action scales and need rescaling for tasks with different action magnitudes.

9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Continuous Action RL|Soft.what_it_is: SAC (Haarnoja et al. 2018) is an off-policy actor-critic algorithm for continuous (and, with adaptations, discrete) action spaces based on the MAXIMUM ENTROPY RL framework: instead of maximizing E[Σγ^t r_t] alone, SAC maximizes E[Σγ^t(r_t+α·H[π(·|s_t)])] -- the standard return PLUS an entropy bonus at every timestep, weighted by a temperature α, learning a STOCHASTIC policy that is as RANDOM as possible while still achieving high reward.
9|🟡 T2 Deep RL|Continuous Action RL|Soft.why_it_exists: DDPG/TD3's deterministic policies require ad-hoc exploration noise and can be brittle/sensitive to hyperparameters. The maximum-entropy framework provides a PRINCIPLED, theoretically-grounded reason for the policy to remain STOCHASTIC: a policy that achieves the SAME expected return while being MORE RANDOM is explicitly PREFERRED (it's more robust to model errors, naturally explores more, and tends to learn more ROBUST/diverse strategies rather than narrow, brittle ones that happen to exploit a specific quirk of the current Q-estimate). SAC combines this entropy-regularized objective with off-policy learning (replay buffer, like DDPG/TD3) for high sample efficiency, and has become one of the most widely-used algorithms for continuous control due to its STRONG PERFORMANCE and RELATIVE INSENSITIVITY to hyperparameters (compared to DDPG/TD3).
