9|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|RL F.why_it_exists: Classic benchmarks (Atari, MuJoCo) test a fixed set of levels/tasks, so an agent can memorize/overfit to specific level layouts without learning genuinely generalizable policies. These suites exist because procedural generation - new layouts every episode - forces agents to learn generalizable strategies rather than memorized solutions, directly testing the 'does it generalize to unseen instances' question central to real-world deployment.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|RL F.how_it_works: MiniGrid environments are lightweight grid-worlds (fast to simulate, ideal for quick iteration) with procedurally placed objects/goals/obstacles and optional language-described missions (BabyAI extension), useful for exploration and instruction-following research. The NetHack Learning Environment wraps the actual NetHack game (a deep, complex roguelike with hundreds of monster/item types, procedurally generated dungeons, and permadeath) as a Gym environment, providing an extremely hard long-horizon, partially-observable, sparse-reward benchmark. Procgen generates 16 distinct game environments (CoinRun, StarPilot, etc.) where each episode uses a new procedurally-generated level from an effectively infinite distribution, with a clean train/test split (e.g., train on levels 0-199, test on levels 200+) to directly measure generalization gap.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|RL F.use_when: Research specifically focused on generalization (does the agent work on unseen levels/configurations, not just memorized ones), exploration in combinatorially large state spaces, or long-horizon planning under partial observability - MiniGrid/Procgen for fast iteration, NetHack for the hardest long-horizon challenge.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|RL F.avoid_when: Benchmarking raw sample efficiency or asymptotic performance on a fixed task (use Atari/MuJoCo, which have decades of comparable published results); NetHack specifically is impractically hard as a first benchmark for a new algorithm - even state-of-the-art agents achieve only a small fraction of human performance.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|RL F.what_goes_wrong: Procgen's generalization gap (train performance vs. test performance) can be large even for well-tuned agents, and naive hyperparameters tuned on Atari often transfer poorly; NetHack's enormous action/observation complexity means most standard RL algorithms make essentially no progress without significant additional structure (hierarchical RL, language-model-based priors, or imitation from human play data); MiniGrid's simplicity can make it too easy for modern algorithms, so it's primarily useful for exploration-focused research rather than general benchmarking.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|RL F.real_example: The NetHack Learning Environment is used as a 'grand challenge' benchmark - even after years of RL research, top agents (often combining RL with symbolic bots or imitation learning) achieve only a fraction of the score of experienced human players, illustrating how far current RL is from human-level long-horizon planning in combinatorially complex environments; Procgen is commonly used to demonstrate that techniques like data augmentation and larger networks measurably reduce the train/test generalization gap.

9|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|RL F.what_it_is: The DeepMind Control Suite (DMControl) is a set of continuous-control benchmark tasks built on the MuJoCo physics engine, providing a standardized collection of locomotion and manipulation tasks (e.g., cheetah-run, walker-walk, humanoid-stand, finger-spin) with consistent reward functions and observation/action specifications for comparing continuous-control algorithms.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|RL F.why_it_exists: While Gymnasium's MuJoCo environments (covered in the earlier Gymnasium note) are widely used, DMControl exists as DeepMind's parallel benchmark suite with a different design philosophy - tasks are organized by difficulty tiers, reward functions are designed to be smooth and well-shaped (avoiding sparse-reward pathologies), and the suite includes both proprioceptive (state-based) and pixel-based observation variants of the same tasks, enabling controlled comparisons of state-based vs. vision-based RL.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|RL F.how_it_works: Each task is defined by a (domain, task) pair (e.g., ('cheetah','run'), ('humanoid','stand')) and returns observations as either a flat proprioceptive vector (joint positions/velocities) or pixel renderings, with a reward in [0,1] computed from a smooth function of the agent's state relative to the task goal (e.g., forward velocity for 'run' tasks). The suite includes the 'Control Suite' (classic tasks) and extensions like the Manipulation suite (object interaction with a robot arm) and Locomotion suite (more complex bodies like quadrupeds and humanoids on varied terrain).
9|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|RL F.use_when: Benchmarking continuous-control algorithms (especially model-based RL and pixel-based RL like Dreamer) with smooth, well-shaped rewards where you want to isolate algorithmic performance from reward-design issues; comparing state-based vs. pixel-based learning on identical underlying tasks.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|RL F.avoid_when: You need environments matching a specific real robot's exact morphology/dynamics for sim-to-real work (use Isaac Gym/Lab or a custom MuJoCo model instead); you want sparse-reward or exploration-focused benchmarks (DMControl's smooth rewards make exploration relatively easy compared to Procgen/NetHack/Montezuma's Revenge).
9|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|RL F.what_goes_wrong: Because DMControl's reward functions are carefully smoothed/shaped, algorithms that perform well on DMControl don't always transfer that performance to sparser-reward real-world tasks - it can give an overly optimistic picture of an algorithm's exploration capability; the pixel-based variants require careful handling of frame stacking/action repeat settings that significantly affect reported results, and papers don't always report these consistently, making cross-paper comparisons tricky.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|RL F.real_example: The Dreamer and DreamerV2/V3 papers report results primarily on DMControl's pixel-based tasks specifically because the suite's paired state/pixel variants of the same underlying task let researchers cleanly measure how much performance is lost (or retained) when learning from images vs. ground-truth state - a comparison that's harder to make cleanly on Gymnasium's MuJoCo environments.

9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.what_it_is: GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) is a policy-gradient RL algorithm, used prominently in DeepSeek's reasoning-model training, that estimates advantages by comparing a group of sampled completions for the same prompt against each other's rewards, eliminating the need for a learned value/critic network.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.why_it_exists: The earlier survey note on 'RL for LLMs' introduces GRPO alongside RLHF/DPO at the level of 'what RL technique does this LLM training stage use'; this note exists to analyze GRPO from the RL-algorithms lineage perspective - as a policy-gradient method descended from REINFORCE-with-baseline and PPO, GRPO exists because training a separate critic/value network (as PPO requires) is expensive and unstable for LLMs with tens of billions of parameters, so GRPO replaces the learned baseline with a cheap, unbiased empirical baseline computed directly from a group of samples.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.how_it_works: For each prompt, sample a group of G completions (e.g., G=64) from the current policy; compute a scalar reward for each (from a reward model or rule-based verifier). The advantage for each completion is its reward normalized relative to the group's mean and standard deviation, A_i = (r_i - mean(r)) / std(r) - this plays exactly the 'baseline' role that a value function plays in PPO, but computed empirically per-prompt instead of learned. Apply PPO's clipped surrogate objective using these group-relative advantages, optionally with a KL penalty to a reference policy.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.use_when: Large-scale LLM RL fine-tuning (RLHF, RLVR for reasoning) where training a separate critic network of comparable size to the policy is computationally prohibitive, and where rewards are available for many samples per prompt cheaply (verifiable rewards like math/code correctness, or a reward model that's cheap to query repeatedly).
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.avoid_when: Settings with very expensive reward evaluation per sample (the group-sampling approach requires G rollouts per prompt, multiplying inference cost); traditional RL settings (robotics, games) where a learned value function is cheap relative to the policy and provides lower-variance advantage estimates than a small empirical group.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.what_goes_wrong: If the group size G is too small or the reward distribution within a group has near-zero variance (e.g., all completions get the same reward - common for easy or impossibly-hard prompts), the normalized advantage becomes noisy or near-zero/undefined, providing no learning signal for that prompt; reward hacking can occur faster than with PPO+critic because there's no value function acting as an implicit regularizer/smoother on the reward signal.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.real_example: DeepSeek-R1's reasoning capabilities (mathematical proofs, code generation) were trained using GRPO with rule-based rewards (did the code pass tests? did the math answer match?), sampling 64 completions per problem and using their relative correctness to compute advantages - avoiding the need to train and maintain a separate ~70B-parameter critic alongside the policy.

9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.what_it_is: Within the broader trend of 'modern RL algorithms' moving toward general-purpose, foundation-model-style agents, DreamerV3's headline result - one fixed configuration solving 150+ tasks across radically different domains (Atari, DMControl, Minecraft, robotics) - represents a qualitative shift from RL's historical norm of per-task hyperparameter tuning toward 'foundation agent' design.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.why_it_exists: Earlier notes cover Dreamer's architecture (latent world model plus actor-critic in imagination) and DreamerV3's specific technical fixes (symlog, free bits); this note exists to address the field-level implication - why 'one config for everything' matters as a research direction, paralleling how LLM scaling showed that one architecture/training recipe could generalize across tasks via scale rather than task-specific design, suggesting RL might follow a similar trajectory toward general agents.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.how_it_works: DreamerV3 demonstrated that performance scales smoothly and predictably with model size (larger world models plus actor-critic networks reliably perform better, with no per-task retuning) - an RL analogue of LLM scaling laws. This predictability is what enables a single config to work everywhere: instead of hand-tuning reward scales, KL weights, or learning rates per environment, the symlog/free-bits/percentile-normalization machinery automatically adapts to each task's statistics, and scaling the network simply improves results monotonically rather than requiring re-tuning.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.use_when: As context for evaluating whether a new RL algorithm/result represents genuine progress toward general-purpose agents (does it require per-task tuning, or does one configuration transfer?) - a key lens for assessing 'modern' RL research; when advocating for investing in larger world-model agents as a strategy rather than algorithm-specific tricks per task.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.avoid_when: Don't extrapolate 'one config works for 150+ benchmark tasks' to 'will work for your specific novel real-world task without any validation' - the 150+ tasks, while diverse, are still simulation benchmarks with relatively well-behaved reward structures; genuinely novel reward structures or observation modalities may still require adaptation.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.what_goes_wrong: The 'no tuning needed' narrative can lead practitioners to skip validation on their specific task, assuming DreamerV3's defaults will 'just work' - while often a strong starting point, real-world deployment (robotics, non-simulated rewards) can still expose edge cases the 150-task benchmark suite didn't cover; the scaling-law framing can also be misapplied to claim that simply using a bigger network fixes fundamentally different problems (e.g., truly sparse-reward exploration) that scale alone doesn't solve.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.real_example: The DreamerV3 paper's headline figure - a single learning curve showing the same algorithm and hyperparameters succeeding on Atari (pixel-based, discrete actions), DMControl (state-based, continuous actions), and Minecraft diamond collection (long-horizon, sparse reward, 3D pixels) - is frequently cited as evidence that 'general agents' via scaled world models are a viable alternative path to the 'general agents via large language models' approach.

9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.what_it_is: Building on the foundational Decision Transformer/Trajectory Transformer idea (RL as sequence modeling), this note covers their evolution into multi-task and multi-game generalist agents - Multi-Game Decision Transformer and DeepMind's Gato - which scale the 'sequence model conditioned on return' recipe across dozens to hundreds of distinct tasks and even multiple modalities (text, images, actions) within a single transformer.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.why_it_exists: The earlier note establishes DT/TT as a single-task offline-RL technique and its limitations (the stitching problem); this note exists to trace where that idea went next - once RL is reframed as sequence modeling, the same transformer that can be scaled for language (GPT-3, GPT-4) can in principle be scaled across many tasks/embodiments simultaneously, which is the 'modern RL algorithms' research direction toward generalist agents that this subtopic covers.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.how_it_works: Multi-Game Decision Transformer trains a single transformer on (return, state, action) sequences from dozens of different Atari games simultaneously, using expert-action-inference techniques (choosing actions the model considers high-likelihood under a high-return context) to mitigate the single-task DT's sensitivity to the specified target return. Gato goes further, tokenizing not just RL trajectories but also images, text, and proprioception from over 600 distinct tasks (Atari, robot manipulation, image captioning, dialogue) into one sequence vocabulary, training a single transformer to handle all of them via the same next-token prediction objective used for DT.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.use_when: As a conceptual reference for the 'generalist agent via sequence modeling' research direction - relevant when discussing whether/how RL can benefit from the same scaling recipes that worked for language models, or when designing multi-task offline RL systems that need to share a single model across many tasks.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.avoid_when: Building a production system for a single, well-defined task - the overhead of multi-task tokenization/training infrastructure isn't justified when a task-specific DT (or even simpler offline RL algorithm) would suffice; don't expect Gato-style generalist agents to match specialist single-task agents on any individual task, since generalists trade peak per-task performance for breadth.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.what_goes_wrong: Multi-task sequence models can suffer from negative transfer, where tasks with conflicting optimal strategies interfere with each other's performance during joint training; tokenization schemes that work for one modality (discretized actions) may be inefficient or lossy for another (continuous robot joint angles vs. discrete Atari actions), requiring careful per-modality tokenizer design; evaluating 'generalist' claims requires care, since reporting average performance across many tasks can mask severe failures on a subset of tasks.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.real_example: Gato (DeepMind, 2022) used a single 1.2B-parameter transformer to play Atari games, caption images, chat in dialogue, and control a real robot arm - all via the same tokenized-sequence-modeling approach pioneered by Decision Transformer, demonstrating (with caveats about per-task performance vs. specialists) that the 'RL as sequence modeling' framing scales toward genuinely multi-modal, multi-task agents.

9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.what_it_is: Conservative Q-Learning (CQL) is an offline RL algorithm that adds a regularization term to standard Q-learning that explicitly pushes down Q-values for actions not seen in the dataset, while pushing up (or leaving unchanged) Q-values for actions that ARE in the dataset - directly counteracting the overestimation of out-of-distribution actions that plagues naive offline Q-learning.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.why_it_exists: The earlier survey note covers CQL as one of three offline RL approaches at a conceptual level ('conservative value estimation'); this note exists to detail how CQL achieves conservatism mechanically - the specific loss function modification - since understanding this mechanism is what lets practitioners debug CQL training (e.g., diagnosing whether the conservative penalty is too strong or weak) and distinguishes CQL's approach from IQL's and BCQ's different mechanisms for achieving the same conservative goal.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.how_it_works: CQL augments the standard Bellman error with a penalty: min_Q [ alpha * (log Sum_a exp(Q(s,a)) - E_{a~dataset}[Q(s,a)]) ] + standard TD loss. The first term (log-sum-exp over all actions) approximates the maximum Q-value over the full action space (including out-of-distribution actions), while the second term is the Q-value for actions actually in the dataset; minimizing their difference pushes down Q-values for actions the policy might exploit but weren't in the data, while keeping in-distribution Q-values accurate via the TD loss. The coefficient alpha controls how conservative the resulting policy is - higher alpha means more conservative (closer to pure imitation of the dataset).
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.use_when: Offline RL on datasets where you need a principled way to prevent the policy from exploiting Q-function errors on out-of-distribution actions, especially when the dataset has diverse/suboptimal trajectories that the policy needs to improve upon (CQL can outperform the data-collection policy, unlike pure imitation).
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.avoid_when: The offline dataset is narrow/near-expert (IQL or behavior cloning may be simpler and equally effective with less tuning); online fine-tuning is available (CQL's conservative penalty can make initial online exploration overly cautious, slowing adaptation compared to less conservative methods).
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.what_goes_wrong: The alpha coefficient is highly sensitive and dataset-dependent - too low and CQL doesn't prevent overestimation (similar to naive offline Q-learning); too high and the policy becomes overly conservative, barely improving on the dataset's average behavior. The log-sum-exp term requires either discretizing the action space (for discrete CQL) or sampling-based approximation (for continuous CQL via importance sampling), and a poor approximation undermines the whole mechanism.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.real_example: On the D4RL 'antmaze' tasks (sparse-reward, requiring stitching together sub-optimal trajectory segments to find a path to the goal), CQL substantially outperforms behavior cloning by using its conservative Q-function to perform genuine dynamic-programming-based improvement over the dataset, while still avoiding the catastrophic overestimation that plain Q-learning exhibits offline.

9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.what_it_is: Implicit Q-Learning (IQL) is an offline RL algorithm that avoids the overestimation problem entirely by never querying the Q-function at out-of-distribution actions - instead, it estimates an implicit state-value function V(s) via expectile regression over the Q-values of in-dataset actions only, sidestepping the need for conservative penalties (CQL) or explicit behavioral constraints (BCQ/BEAR).
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.why_it_exists: The earlier survey note groups IQL alongside CQL and TD3+BC as 'offline RL approaches'; this note exists to highlight IQL's distinctively different mechanism - rather than adding a penalty (CQL) or constraining the policy to stay near the data (BCQ/BEAR), IQL changes what is being estimated so out-of-distribution actions never enter the computation at all, making it simpler to implement and tune (fewer hyperparameters than CQL) while often matching or exceeding CQL's performance.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.how_it_works: IQL trains a value function V(s) using expectile regression against Q(s,a) for actions a actually in the dataset: L(V) = E_(s,a)~D [ L2_tau(Q(s,a) - V(s)) ], where L2_tau is an asymmetric loss that weights positive errors (Q > V) by tau and negative errors by (1-tau); setting tau close to 1 makes V(s) approximate the maximum Q-value over in-dataset actions (an implicit max, without ever evaluating Q at out-of-distribution actions). The Q-function is then trained via standard TD learning using this V(s) as the bootstrap target, and a separate policy is extracted afterward via advantage-weighted regression (favoring actions with high A(s,a) = Q(s,a) - V(s)).
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.use_when: As a strong, relatively simple-to-tune default for offline RL - fewer hyperparameters than CQL (mainly just the expectile tau), works well across both narrow/near-expert and diverse datasets, and is straightforward to combine with online fine-tuning afterward (since it doesn't rely on a conservative penalty that needs to be 'turned off' for online adaptation).
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.avoid_when: Tasks where the implicit max via expectile regression with a fixed tau doesn't capture enough of the actual best-case actions (very sparse, narrow optimal-action regions might need tau very close to 1, which can become numerically unstable); if you need explicit uncertainty quantification over actions, CQL's explicit penalty formulation can be more interpretable.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.what_goes_wrong: Choosing tau too close to 1 (trying to approximate a hard max) can make the expectile regression numerically unstable and overly optimistic if the dataset has few samples per state; the separate policy-extraction step (advantage-weighted regression) is itself an approximation - a poorly calibrated extraction can fail to recover the policy implied by the learned V/Q even if those are accurate; IQL's simplicity can be deceptive, since it still requires the dataset to have reasonable state-action coverage near the optimal policy for the implicit max to be meaningful.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.real_example: IQL is commonly used as the offline pretraining step before online fine-tuning in robot learning pipelines - because it doesn't rely on a conservative penalty term that actively suppresses Q-values for unseen actions, switching to online data collection and continuing to train doesn't require re-tuning a penalty coefficient, making the offline-to-online transition smoother than with CQL.

9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.what_it_is: BCQ (Batch-Constrained Q-learning) and BEAR (Bootstrapping Error Accumulation Reduction) are offline RL algorithms that constrain the learned policy to select actions similar to those in the training dataset, using a generative model (BCQ) or a distributional distance penalty (BEAR) to prevent the policy from querying the Q-function at unfamiliar actions where its estimates are unreliable.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.why_it_exists: Before CQL and IQL's value-function-centric solutions, BCQ and BEAR were among the first algorithms to identify and address the core offline RL problem - Q-learning's bootstrapping process repeatedly queries Q(s',a') for actions a' chosen by the current policy, and if the policy drifts toward actions absent from the dataset, these Q-value estimates are extrapolation errors that compound over training ('bootstrapping error accumulation'). They exist to constrain the policy directly (rather than the value function) to stay within the support of the data distribution.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.how_it_works: BCQ trains a conditional VAE (generative model) to model the dataset's action distribution given a state; at action-selection time, it samples a small number of candidate actions from this VAE (perturbed slightly by a learned perturbation model), then picks the one with the highest learned Q-value - effectively restricting the action search to a region near what the data distribution supports. BEAR instead adds an explicit penalty to the policy's objective based on the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) between the learned policy's action distribution and the dataset's behavior-policy action distribution at each state, allowing some flexibility (unlike BCQ's hard generative constraint) while still discouraging large distributional shift.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.use_when: Historical/conceptual reference for understanding the offline RL problem space and the 'constrain the policy directly' family of solutions; BEAR's MMD-based distributional constraint is occasionally still used when a softer constraint than BCQ's generative-model restriction is desired but CQL/IQL aren't a good fit for the specific architecture.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.avoid_when: For new offline RL projects, CQL and especially IQL are generally simpler to implement, more robust to hyperparameters, and at least as performant - BCQ's VAE training adds an extra model to tune, and BEAR's MMD distance computation is sensitive to kernel choice and bandwidth; both are mostly superseded in practice.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.what_goes_wrong: BCQ's VAE can fail to capture multimodal action distributions well - if the dataset contains multiple distinct strategies for the same state, the VAE may generate a blended, invalid 'average' action, the same multimodality problem that motivates Diffusion Policy in imitation learning; BEAR's MMD penalty requires careful kernel/bandwidth selection, and an overly strict constraint reduces BEAR to behavior cloning while too loose a constraint reverts to standard Q-learning's extrapolation problems.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.real_example: BCQ was the first algorithm to demonstrate that 'just running standard off-policy RL (DDPG/SAC) on a fixed dataset without online interaction' fails catastrophically due to extrapolation error, and that constraining actions to the data-supported region recovers reasonable performance - this finding directly motivated the entire offline RL subfield, including the later CQL/IQL approaches covered elsewhere in this curriculum.

9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.what_it_is: SEED RL (Scalable, Efficient Deep-RL) is an evolution of IMPALA's actor-learner architecture that moves neural network inference (action selection) from the distributed actors onto the central learner's accelerators (TPUs/GPUs), with actors becoming lightweight processes that only run the environment and stream observations to/from the learner over fast RPC.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.why_it_exists: The earlier note covers IMPALA's actor-learner split, where each actor runs its own copy of the policy network for inference (on CPU) and only sends completed trajectories to the learner; this works but wastes accelerator utilization (the learner GPU/TPU sits partly idle waiting for CPU-bound actors) and requires distributing model weights to every actor repeatedly. SEED RL exists to fix this inefficiency by centralizing both inference and learning on the accelerator, with actors reduced to pure environment-stepping processes - dramatically improving accelerator utilization and reducing the data/weight transfer overhead that limited IMPALA's scaling.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.how_it_works: Each actor process runs only the environment, sending observations to the learner via gRPC and receiving back the selected action; the learner runs a batched inference step for all actors' observations simultaneously on TPU/GPU (since modern accelerators are most efficient with large batches), then performs the standard IMPALA-style V-trace learning update on the resulting trajectories. Because inference happens on the same accelerator and weights as training, there's no need to serialize/transfer model weights to actors, and the accelerator stays highly utilized doing both inference and learning in tight succession.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.use_when: Extremely large-scale distributed RL where accelerator utilization and network bandwidth (for weight distribution) are the bottlenecks - massive Atari-scale or simulation-scale training with thousands of actors where IMPALA's per-actor inference becomes the limiting factor.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.avoid_when: Small-to-medium scale training where IMPALA's simpler architecture (actors with local inference) is sufficient and the added complexity of streaming every observation over RPC to a centralized inference server isn't justified; environments with very high-dimensional observations (e.g., high-resolution images) where the network bandwidth to stream observations to the learner becomes its own bottleneck.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.what_goes_wrong: The RPC round-trip latency for every observation/action exchange can become a bottleneck if not carefully pipelined (SEED RL addresses this with asynchronous, batched RPC, but naive implementations can stall); centralizing inference means a learner failure/restart affects all actors simultaneously, unlike IMPALA where actors can continue locally for a while with slightly stale weights; the architecture is significantly more complex to set up and debug than IMPALA's already-complex distributed pipeline.
9|🟡 T2 🔬 Modern RL Algorithms|Modern RL.real_example: Google's SEED RL paper demonstrated training Atari and DMLab agents at significantly higher throughput (millions of frames per second) than IMPALA on the same hardware budget, by keeping TPUs continuously busy with batched inference and learning rather than having them wait on CPU actors - directly enabling the kind of massive-scale experiments (e.g., training on all 57 Atari games or large 3D environments) that motivated IMPALA in the first place, but with better hardware efficiency.

9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.what_it_is: Random Network Distillation (RND) is an exploration bonus method that uses the prediction error of a neural network trying to predict the output of a fixed, randomly-initialized 'target' network as an intrinsic reward - states where the predictor network performs poorly (novel/unvisited states) get higher intrinsic reward.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.why_it_exists: The earlier 'Curiosity-driven exploration' note introduces RND as one of several intrinsic-motivation techniques (alongside ICM and count-based methods) at a survey level; this note exists to detail RND's specific mechanism and why it became one of the most widely-adopted curiosity methods - notably, RND doesn't require learning a forward/inverse dynamics model (unlike ICM), making it simpler, more stable, and immune to the 'noisy TV problem' in a different way than ICM.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.how_it_works: A fixed, randomly-initialized target network f(s) (never trained) maps observations to a feature vector; a separate predictor network f-hat(s) is trained to minimize ||f-hat(s) - f(s)||^2 via supervised learning on visited states. The prediction error itself is used as the intrinsic reward - since f is fixed and random, the predictor's error on a given state decreases monotonically with how many times that state (or similar states) has been visited, naturally giving high reward to novel states and low reward to familiar ones, without needing any notion of 'dynamics' or 'action prediction'.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.use_when: Sparse-reward exploration problems (Montezuma's Revenge-style games, hard-exploration robotics) where you want a simple, stable intrinsic-motivation signal that's cheap to compute (one extra small network, no dynamics model); as a drop-in addition to PPO/DQN-style agents via an auxiliary reward term.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.avoid_when: Environments where pixel-level novelty doesn't correlate with task-relevant novelty (RND can still be fooled by visually complex but task-irrelevant variation, e.g., background animations, although less severely than ICM's 'noisy TV' problem); dense-reward tasks where extrinsic reward alone provides sufficient exploration signal, since the added intrinsic reward just adds noise.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.what_goes_wrong: The intrinsic reward scale needs careful balancing against the extrinsic reward (typically via separate value heads/discount factors for intrinsic vs. extrinsic rewards, as in the original RND paper, rather than simply summing them); RND's novelty signal decays over training as the predictor learns to match the target everywhere, which can cause exploration to taper off before the task is fully solved if intrinsic reward isn't the only exploration mechanism; running mean/std normalization of the intrinsic reward is essential and easy to get wrong, since non-stationary normalization statistics can destabilize training.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.real_example: RND was the first method to achieve non-trivial scores on Montezuma's Revenge (a notoriously hard-exploration Atari game requiring long sequences of precise actions before any reward) without using human demonstrations, by providing a steady stream of novelty-based intrinsic rewards that guided the agent through previously unvisited rooms.

9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.what_it_is: The Intrinsic Curiosity Module (ICM) generates an exploration bonus based on how poorly a learned forward-dynamics model can predict the consequences of the agent's actions in a learned feature space - the agent is rewarded for visiting states where its own action-effect predictions are most wrong.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.why_it_exists: The earlier 'Curiosity-driven exploration' note covers ICM as one member of the intrinsic-motivation family; this note exists to detail ICM's specific two-network mechanism (forward model plus inverse model) and its key innovation - learning a feature representation specifically designed to ignore aspects of the observation the agent's actions can't influence, which is ICM's attempted (partial) solution to the 'noisy TV problem' that plagues naively pixel-based curiosity.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.how_it_works: ICM trains two networks jointly: an inverse model that takes consecutive states (s_t, s_{t+1}) and predicts the action a_t that caused the transition, forcing a learned feature encoder phi(s) to capture only action-relevant aspects of the observation (ignoring irrelevant background noise that no action affects); a forward model that takes phi(s_t) and a_t and predicts phi(s_{t+1}). The prediction error of the forward model, ||phi-hat(s_{t+1}) - phi(s_{t+1})||^2, is the intrinsic reward - high when the agent encounters action-state combinations whose effects it can't yet predict.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.use_when: Exploration problems where some parts of the observation are inherently unpredictable/irrelevant (so raw pixel-prediction-error curiosity would be fooled) but the agent's actions DO have predictable effects on task-relevant features; visual navigation/exploration tasks where the inverse-model's action-relevant feature learning helps focus curiosity on the agent's own movement effects.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.avoid_when: The 'noisy TV problem' is severe and not adequately solved by the inverse-model feature learning (a TV showing random video the agent can walk toward, even if it can't control it, can still produce persistently high forward-model error since the agent's proximity correlates loosely with the prediction target) - RND's simpler fixed-random-target approach is often more robust in practice; tasks with very high-dimensional continuous action spaces where the inverse model (predicting actions from state transitions) is itself hard to learn accurately.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.what_goes_wrong: The forward and inverse models can develop a degenerate equilibrium where the feature encoder collapses to a trivial representation (everything maps to similar features), making both losses small without the agent having learned anything useful - requires careful loss-weighting and architecture choices to avoid; ICM's curiosity signal, like RND's, decays as the forward model improves, so it can stop providing useful signal partway through training on very long-horizon tasks.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.real_example: ICM enabled an agent in VizDoom (a 3D first-person environment) to learn to navigate toward a distant goal purely from curiosity-driven exploration with the extrinsic reward turned off entirely, demonstrating that the action-conditioned forward-model error alone can drive meaningful exploration behavior - a capability the original ICM paper used to argue curiosity could serve as a general-purpose exploration signal independent of task reward.

9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.what_it_is: Go-Explore is an exploration algorithm for extremely hard-exploration problems that explicitly maintains an archive of previously-visited states ('cells'), and explores by first deterministically returning to a promising previously-visited state (via a saved trajectory or a learned 'go-to' policy), then exploring randomly or with a policy from that point - separating 'getting back to the frontier of exploration' from 'exploring beyond it'.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.why_it_exists: Standard exploration methods (epsilon-greedy, intrinsic motivation like RND/ICM) can suffer from 'detachment' (the agent forgets how to get back to a promising area it discovered) and 'derailment' (random exploration noise prevents the agent from reliably returning to a known good state). Go-Explore exists to directly solve both problems by explicitly remembering interesting states and how to reach them, achieving breakthrough results on the hardest sparse-reward Atari games where RND/ICM-style intrinsic motivation alone made little progress.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.how_it_works: Phase 1 ('Explore'): maintain an archive mapping discretized state representations ('cells', e.g., downsampled images) to the best trajectory found so far that reaches that cell; repeatedly select a cell (weighted toward less-visited/promising ones), restore the environment to that state (using a simulator that supports save/restore, or a learned policy to return there), then take a short sequence of random actions, updating the archive with any newly-discovered cells or better trajectories. Phase 2 ('Robustify'): train a neural network policy via imitation learning/RL to robustly reproduce the best trajectory found, so it works even with the stochasticity/domain randomization the deterministic Phase-1 trajectory might not handle.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.use_when: Extremely hard sparse-reward exploration problems where intrinsic-motivation methods (RND, ICM) plateau - the canonical case is Montezuma's Revenge and Pitfall, where Go-Explore was the first method to exceed average human performance; settings where you have simulator access that supports state save/restore, needed for Phase 1's deterministic return.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.avoid_when: Environments without save/restore access or with significant stochasticity that makes 'returning to exactly this state' ill-defined (real robots, for instance) - Go-Explore's original formulation relies heavily on simulator determinism, though later variants address this with learned 'go-to' policies; tasks that aren't actually hard-exploration problems, where Go-Explore's archive/cell machinery is substantial overhead unnecessary for simpler exploration.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.what_goes_wrong: The choice of 'cell' representation (how states are discretized/grouped) is critical and somewhat task-specific - too coarse and distinct important states get merged, missing exploration opportunities; too fine and the archive explodes in size without meaningful generalization. Relying on simulator determinism/save-restore in Phase 1 means discovered trajectories may be brittle 'overfit' solutions that the Phase 2 robustification step must repair, and that repair isn't always fully successful.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.real_example: Go-Explore was the first algorithm to solve Montezuma's Revenge (achieving scores far exceeding average human play, and even finding the game's secret 'kill screen' beyond all 24 levels) and Pitfall (where every prior RL method, including RND, scored near zero), by explicitly remembering and returning to the frontier of explored states rather than relying purely on a moment-to-moment intrinsic reward signal.

9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.what_it_is: NoisyNets and parameter-space noise are exploration techniques that inject learnable or fixed noise directly into a network's weights (rather than into its output actions, as epsilon-greedy or Gaussian action noise does), producing exploration that is consistent within an episode and naturally state-dependent.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.why_it_exists: The earlier Rainbow DQN note mentions NoisyNets as one of Rainbow's six components without detailing the mechanism; this note exists to explain how and why weight-space noise differs fundamentally from action-space noise (epsilon-greedy) - epsilon-greedy's random action choice is independent of the state and uncorrelated across timesteps (so exploration looks like jittery, inconsistent behavior), whereas noise in the weights produces a temporarily-fixed 'noisy version' of the policy applied consistently across an episode (or until resampled), giving more coherent, state-dependent exploratory behavior (e.g., consistently exploring 'go left more' for a while, rather than randomly flipping left/right every step).
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.how_it_works: NoisyNets replace standard linear layers y = Wx + b with noisy linear layers y = (W + sigma_W * eps_W)x + (b + sigma_b * eps_b), where eps are noise variables (resampled periodically, e.g., every step or every episode) and sigma are learnable parameters the network adjusts via gradient descent - the network learns how much noise/exploration is useful per-parameter, and can reduce sigma toward zero for parameters where exploration isn't beneficial, effectively annealing exploration automatically rather than requiring a hand-tuned epsilon schedule. Parameter-space noise (a related, earlier technique) instead perturbs network weights with fixed-variance Gaussian noise, with the variance adapted based on how much the noisy policy's behavior differs from the non-noisy policy (measured via action-distribution distance).
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.use_when: As a drop-in replacement for epsilon-greedy in value-based methods (DQN and variants) or as an exploration mechanism for policy-gradient methods, when you want exploration that's automatically tuned (no epsilon schedule to hand-design) and more temporally consistent than per-step random action selection.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.avoid_when: Continuous-control algorithms that already have principled exploration via stochastic policies with entropy regularization (SAC) - adding NoisyNets on top is usually redundant; environments where the optimal exploration strategy genuinely is per-step-independent randomness (rare, but epsilon-greedy's simplicity may suffice).
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.what_goes_wrong: NoisyNets roughly double the number of parameters in affected layers (separate sigma for each weight/bias), increasing memory and compute; the learnable noise scale sigma can sometimes collapse toward zero early in training if the network finds a locally-good deterministic policy, prematurely ending exploration before better solutions are found; parameter-space noise's adaptive variance mechanism requires an additional distance metric and adaptation rate that introduces its own hyperparameters.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.real_example: In Rainbow DQN's ablation studies, removing NoisyNets caused one of the larger performance drops among the six components on exploration-heavy Atari games, confirming that weight-space noise's state-consistent exploration provides meaningfully different (and often better) exploration behavior than the epsilon-greedy schedule it replaced.

9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.what_it_is: Bootstrapped DQN is an exploration method that trains an ensemble of K Q-value 'heads' sharing a common feature backbone, each head trained on a different bootstrapped (resampled) subset of experience, where the disagreement between heads serves as an implicit measure of uncertainty that drives deep, temporally-consistent exploration; 'prior networks' add a fixed random network to each head to maintain useful uncertainty even after the ensemble would otherwise converge to agreement.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.why_it_exists: Epsilon-greedy and even NoisyNets produce exploration that's largely independent across timesteps (the agent might explore 'left' at one step and 'right' the next with no relationship), which is poorly suited to problems requiring a consistent sequence of exploratory actions (e.g., committing to explore down a long corridor). Bootstrapped DQN exists to produce 'deep exploration' - exploration strategies that commit to a particular exploratory hypothesis (a particular Q-head) for an entire episode, enabling the kind of multi-step coordinated exploration needed for long-horizon sparse-reward tasks.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.how_it_works: A shared convolutional/feature backbone feeds into K separate Q-value heads, each trained on a different random bootstrap mask of each transition (so each head effectively sees a different resampled dataset, like a bootstrap ensemble in statistics); at the start of each episode, one head is selected uniformly at random and used for all action selections in that episode (greedy w.r.t. that head's Q-values, no epsilon needed) - since different heads may disagree about which actions are good in under-explored regions, this produces episode-consistent exploration that varies head-to-head. 'Prior networks' add a fixed, randomly-initialized, untrained network's output to each head's prediction, ensuring that even if all heads converge to the same trained values, the added random priors maintain a baseline level of inter-head disagreement (uncertainty) in under-visited regions.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.use_when: Long-horizon, sparse-reward tasks where temporally-consistent ('deep') exploration matters - committing to explore a particular direction/strategy for many steps rather than randomizing each step independently; as a Bayesian-inspired approach to uncertainty-driven exploration without the computational cost of full Bayesian neural networks.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.avoid_when: Short-horizon tasks or dense-reward tasks where simple per-step exploration (epsilon-greedy, NoisyNets) is already sufficient, since the K-head ensemble adds K-fold compute/memory overhead for the Q-heads; tasks where the shared-backbone assumption is problematic, if the different exploration strategies implied by different heads would benefit from entirely different feature representations rather than just different output heads.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.what_goes_wrong: The number of heads K is a tradeoff - too few heads provide limited diversity/uncertainty signal, too many multiply compute cost with diminishing returns; if the shared backbone is updated by gradients from all heads' losses, it can converge to a representation that doesn't preserve enough diversity for the heads to meaningfully disagree, undermining the whole mechanism (precisely the problem 'prior networks' were added to fix); selecting a new head only at episode boundaries means within-episode adaptation to new information is limited until the next episode starts.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.real_example: Bootstrapped DQN with randomized prior functions showed substantially faster learning than epsilon-greedy DQN on a 'deep sea' sparse-reward exploration benchmark specifically designed to require many consecutive correct exploratory actions to reach any reward - a regime where epsilon-greedy's per-step-independent randomness has exponentially small probability of ever reaching the reward, while bootstrapped DQN's episode-consistent head selection can systematically explore different 'paths' across episodes.

9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.what_it_is: Hash-based pseudo-count exploration extends classic count-based exploration bonuses (which require small, discrete state spaces to maintain visit counts N(s)) to large or continuous/high-dimensional state spaces (like images) by hashing states into a much smaller discrete space, so approximate visit counts can still be tracked and used to compute an exploration bonus like 1/sqrt(N(s)).
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.why_it_exists: The earlier curiosity-driven exploration note mentions count-based methods as one family of intrinsic-motivation approaches alongside ICM/RND at a survey level; this note exists to address the core practical obstacle to count-based exploration - in environments with image observations or continuous states, literally no state ever repeats exactly, so N(s) is always 0 or 1 and provides no useful signal. Hashing solves this by mapping similar states to the same hash bucket, making 'visit counts' meaningful again.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.how_it_works: States are passed through a hash function (e.g., a learned autoencoder's bottleneck layer, binarized and hashed via SimHash, or a random projection followed by discretization) that maps high-dimensional observations to a much smaller discrete code; a count table tracks how many times each hash code has been seen. The exploration bonus for a state is typically 1/sqrt(N(hash(s))) (similar to UCB-style bonuses in bandits/tabular RL), added to the extrinsic reward to encourage visiting under-counted regions of the hashed state space.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.use_when: As a simple, interpretable baseline exploration bonus for environments with high-dimensional observations, especially when you want a bonus with a clear theoretical grounding - count-based bonuses connect directly to UCB/optimism-based exploration theory in bandits and tabular RL, unlike the more heuristic prediction-error bonuses of ICM/RND.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.avoid_when: The hash function's granularity doesn't align with task-relevant state similarity - if the hash collapses meaningfully-different states together (too coarse) the bonus becomes uninformative, and if it's too fine it degenerates back to the 'every state is novel' problem that motivated hashing in the first place; in practice, RND often outperforms hash-based counts on complex visual domains since it doesn't require hand-designing a hash/discretization scheme.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.what_goes_wrong: Choosing the hash granularity (e.g., the dimensionality of the SimHash code, or the autoencoder bottleneck size) requires tuning, and the right granularity can vary across different parts of the same environment (some regions need fine-grained distinction, others don't); hash collisions between genuinely different but co-located states can cause the bonus to under-reward truly novel states that happen to hash the same as previously-visited ones; the count table itself can grow large in long training runs, requiring approximate/hashed count data structures (e.g., count-min sketches) that introduce their own approximation error.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Exploration (Complete)|Explorat.real_example: Hash-based counts (using a SimHash of a learned state encoding) were among the first methods to provide meaningful exploration bonuses on Atari games with raw pixel observations, achieving competitive results with early curiosity-based methods on hard-exploration games like Freeway and Frostbite, by effectively discretizing the pixel-observation space into a manageable number of 'visited region' buckets.

9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.what_it_is: A comparative decision framework for choosing among MADDPG, QMIX, and MAPPO - three of the most widely-used multi-agent RL algorithms - based on the structure of the multi-agent problem: continuous vs. discrete actions, cooperative vs. competitive/mixed, and whether a single joint value function or per-agent values is more appropriate.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.why_it_exists: The earlier Advanced RL note introduces each algorithm's basic mechanism individually; this note exists because in practice the key skill is choosing the right one for a given multi-agent setting - the three algorithms target different points in the cooperative/competitive and discrete/continuous design space, and picking the wrong one (e.g., using MADDPG's per-agent critics for a fully-cooperative team-reward problem where QMIX's factored value function would work better) leads to unnecessarily hard credit-assignment problems.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.how_it_works: MADDPG extends DDPG to multi-agent settings with continuous actions - each agent has its own actor and critic, but each critic is 'centralized' (sees all agents' observations and actions during training), suitable for mixed cooperative-competitive settings (e.g., predator-prey) with continuous control. QMIX targets fully-cooperative settings with discrete actions and a shared team reward - it learns per-agent Q-values combined via a learned 'mixing network' constrained to be monotonic in each agent's Q-value, guaranteeing the joint-action argmax decomposes into independent per-agent argmaxes (enabling decentralized execution while preserving some coordination). MAPPO applies PPO's clipped-objective recipe to multi-agent settings with a centralized critic (seeing the global state) and decentralized actors (each seeing only local observations) - simple, robust, and surprisingly competitive with more complex specialized algorithms across both cooperative discrete and continuous benchmarks.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.use_when: MADDPG for continuous-action, mixed cooperative-competitive multi-agent problems (multi-robot coordination with some competitive elements); QMIX for fully-cooperative discrete-action problems with a shared team reward where the monotonicity assumption (better individual contributions lead to better team outcomes) roughly holds (e.g., StarCraft II micromanagement); MAPPO as a strong, simple-to-implement default for almost any multi-agent setting (cooperative or competitive, discrete or continuous) when you want PPO's robustness and don't need QMIX's specific value-factorization guarantees.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.avoid_when: QMIX's monotonicity constraint can be actively harmful in settings with strong negative interactions between agents (where one agent's improvement could require another's contribution to decrease) - MAPPO or MADDPG may handle these better; MADDPG's per-agent critics scale poorly as the number of agents grows (each critic's input grows with all agents' observations/actions), so for large agent counts MAPPO's shared centralized critic or QMIX's factorization scale better.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.what_goes_wrong: QMIX's monotonic mixing network can fail to represent the true joint action-value function in problems requiring agents to make coordinated sacrifices (the 'relative overgeneralization' problem) - symptoms include the team converging to a suboptimal equilibrium where no single agent's unilateral deviation helps. MADDPG's centralized critics need access to all agents' observations/actions during training, which can be impractical if agents are trained by different organizations that can't share data. MAPPO, despite its simplicity, still requires careful reward design - shared team rewards in cooperative MAPPO can suffer from the same credit-assignment ambiguity as single-agent sparse rewards, just across agents instead of across time.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.real_example: QMIX was the standard baseline for the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC) for years due to its strong performance on discrete, fully-cooperative micromanagement tasks; MAPPO later matched or exceeded QMIX on the same SMAC benchmarks with a much simpler algorithm, leading many practitioners to default to MAPPO first and only reach for QMIX's specialized factorization when MAPPO underperforms.

9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.what_it_is: Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE) is the dominant paradigm in cooperative multi-agent RL - during training, algorithms have access to global information (all agents' observations, actions, and a shared reward signal), but during execution (deployment), each agent acts using only its own local observations, with no communication or access to other agents' information.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.why_it_exists: Fully decentralized training (each agent learns independently from only its own observations) suffers from non-stationarity - from any single agent's perspective, the environment's dynamics appear to change constantly as other agents simultaneously update their policies, making learning unstable. Fully centralized execution (a single controller deciding all agents' actions) requires real-time communication/coordination infrastructure that's often impractical (latency, bandwidth, partial connectivity) and doesn't scale to large agent counts. CTDE exists as the practical middle ground: use the simulator's 'god's eye view' during training (where extra information is free) to learn coordinated policies, but ensure the final policies each agent runs require only locally-available information, making them deployable in realistic decentralized settings.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.how_it_works: During training, a centralized critic (MADDPG, MAPPO) or centralized value-decomposition network (QMIX, VDN) has access to the joint observation/action space of all agents and the global/team reward, providing a stable learning signal that accounts for other agents' behavior; each agent's policy (actor), however, is a function of only that agent's local observation. After training, the centralized critic/mixing network is discarded, and each agent's actor is deployed independently - at execution time, agent i computes its action purely from its own observation o_i, with no access to other agents' observations, the global state, or the now-discarded centralized critic.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.use_when: Cooperative multi-agent problems where training happens in simulation (where global state is freely available) but deployment must work with realistic sensing/communication constraints (robots with limited sensor range, no reliable inter-robot communication); essentially the default paradigm for any cooperative MARL algorithm (QMIX, MADDPG, MAPPO all follow CTDE).
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.avoid_when: If your deployment environment actually supports full communication/centralized control (e.g., a single data center controlling all agents with negligible latency), a fully-centralized approach (treating the whole multi-agent system as one big single-agent problem) might be simpler and not need CTDE's decentralization constraint at all; if even training-time access to global state/other agents' actions is unavailable (e.g., independently-developed agents from different organizations that can't share training data), CTDE isn't applicable and fully decentralized/independent learning is the only option.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.what_goes_wrong: The 'centralized training' assumption requires a simulator or training setup where global information genuinely is available - if real-world data collection can't provide this (e.g., you can only observe one robot's sensors at a time), you can't actually do CTDE despite wanting to; there's sometimes a train/execution mismatch where policies that rely subtly on patterns only present during centralized training (e.g., implicit assumptions baked in via the centralized critic's gradients) perform worse than expected once the centralized component is removed at deployment.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.real_example: A warehouse robot fleet is trained in simulation where the training algorithm (e.g., QMIX) has access to every robot's position, the full warehouse map, and the team's total task-completion reward; once trained, each robot is deployed running only its own actor network, making decisions from its own onboard sensors with no inter-robot communication - exactly the CTDE pattern that makes simulation-trained coordination deployable on real, communication-limited hardware.

9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.what_it_is: PettingZoo is the standard API and library of environments for multi-agent reinforcement learning, providing a Gymnasium-like interface extended for multiple agents - supporting both 'Parallel' (all agents act simultaneously) and 'AEC' (Agent-Environment-Cycle, agents act in turns) environment styles, alongside a large collection of pre-built multi-agent environments (classic games, Atari multiplayer, MPE particle environments, SISL/Butterfly cooperative tasks).
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.why_it_exists: Gymnasium's single-agent Env interface (step(action) -> obs, reward, ...) doesn't naturally extend to multiple agents - questions like 'do all agents act simultaneously or in turn?', 'what happens when one agent's episode ends but others continue?', and 'how are per-agent rewards/observations structured?' have no single standard answer. PettingZoo exists to provide that standard, analogous to how Gymnasium standardized single-agent RL, so multi-agent algorithms (MAPPO, QMIX implementations in RLlib/Tianshou) and environments can interoperate.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.how_it_works: The AEC (Agent-Environment-Cycle) API models environments as a strict turn-based loop where exactly one agent acts at a time (env.step(action) advances to the next agent), naturally handling turn-based games (chess, poker) and variable numbers of active agents; the Parallel API has all agents submit actions simultaneously (env.step({agent: action for agent in agents}) returns a dict of observations/rewards per agent), more natural for simultaneous-move games and most cooperative robotics-style tasks. Both APIs handle agents being added/removed dynamically (e.g., an agent 'dying' mid-episode) and provide wrappers to convert between AEC and Parallel representations where possible.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.use_when: Building or benchmarking multi-agent RL algorithms that need a standard environment interface compatible with multi-agent RL libraries (RLlib's multi-agent API, Tianshou's multi-agent wrappers, MARLlib); prototyping new multi-agent environments where you want compatibility with existing MARL training infrastructure without inventing a custom API.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.avoid_when: Single-agent problems (use plain Gymnasium); extremely large-scale agent populations (hundreds/thousands of agents) where PettingZoo's per-agent dictionary-based observation/action handling may have overhead - specialized large-population frameworks may be more efficient.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.what_goes_wrong: Choosing AEC vs. Parallel incorrectly for your problem's true structure (e.g., forcing a simultaneous-move game into AEC's turn-based model, or vice versa) can introduce subtle behavioral differences from the 'real' game/task; handling variable agent populations (agents joining/leaving) correctly in downstream RL algorithms requires careful handling of the per-agent dictionaries, and bugs here (e.g., forgetting to remove a 'dead' agent from the action dict) are a common source of errors.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.real_example: The Multi-Agent Particle Environments (MPE), used in the original MADDPG paper for tasks like cooperative navigation and predator-prey, are distributed as PettingZoo environments, allowing researchers to benchmark new multi-agent algorithms (implemented in RLlib, Tianshou, or custom code) against the same standardized tasks the original algorithms were evaluated on.

9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.what_it_is: PSRO (Policy-Space Response Oracles) is a self-play algorithm that maintains a growing population of policies and iteratively computes a meta-strategy (a Nash-equilibrium-like distribution over the population) using game-theoretic methods, then trains a new 'best response' policy against that meta-strategy and adds it to the population - addressing non-transitive strategy cycles that plain self-play can get stuck in.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.why_it_exists: The earlier Advanced RL note on self-play (AlphaGo/AlphaZero) covers the basic idea of training against past versions of yourself; this note exists because plain self-play (always play against your most recent self, or a single opponent) can fail in games with non-transitive dynamics - like rock-paper-scissors, where beating 'rock' makes you a 'paper' specialist, who then loses to a 'scissors' specialist that beats you, in an endless cycle that never converges to a robust, generally-strong policy. PSRO exists to escape these cycles by reasoning about the whole population of strategies game-theoretically.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.how_it_works: PSRO maintains a population of policies and a payoff matrix recording how each policy performs against every other; at each iteration, it computes a meta-strategy - a probability distribution over the current population that approximates a Nash equilibrium (e.g., via linear programming for two-player zero-sum games, or replicator dynamics/projected gradient for general cases) - then trains a new policy as a 'best response' against an opponent sampled from this meta-strategy distribution (rather than against a single fixed opponent), adds the new policy to the population, updates the payoff matrix, and repeats. Because the meta-strategy accounts for the whole population's interactions, the new best-response policy is robust against a mixture of past strategies rather than overfitting to beat just the most recent one.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.use_when: Competitive multi-agent games where strategies can cycle non-transitively (most real competitive games beyond simple ones); when you need a final policy that performs robustly against a diverse range of opponents rather than one that's only good against itself; large-scale competitive training where you want a principled way to manage a growing population of diverse strategies (training 'leagues').
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.avoid_when: Fully cooperative multi-agent problems (no adversarial dynamics to manage - use MAPPO/QMIX instead); simple competitive games where transitive 'stronger beats weaker' dynamics dominate and plain self-play already converges reliably without cycling, making PSRO's population-management overhead unnecessary.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.what_goes_wrong: Computing exact Nash equilibria becomes computationally intractable as the policy population grows (the payoff matrix grows quadratically, and equilibrium computation can be expensive for general-sum, many-player games) - practical implementations use approximations (e.g., alpha-rank, or restricting to a subset of the population); maintaining and training against a large population is computationally expensive (each new policy requires evaluation against the whole existing population to update the payoff matrix), and population diversity can collapse if the best-response training repeatedly converges to similar policies.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.real_example: DeepMind's AlphaStar used a 'league' training approach inspired by PSRO principles for StarCraft II - maintaining a population of 'main agents', 'main exploiters' (trained specifically to beat the current main agents' weaknesses), and 'league exploiters' (trained to find weaknesses across the whole league), with a meta-strategy determining matchmaking - producing a final agent robust against a huge diversity of human strategies rather than one that cycles between exploitable styles.

9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.what_it_is: FeUdal Networks (FuN) and HIRO (HIerarchical Reinforcement learning with Off-policy correction) are deep hierarchical RL architectures that extend the classical options framework (covered in the Advanced RL note) by learning a continuous, learned 'goal space' for a high-level policy to communicate with a low-level policy, rather than relying on hand-specified discrete options/sub-goals.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.why_it_exists: The earlier Advanced RL note on the options framework covers the classical formulation - a high-level policy chooses among a discrete set of options (each a sub-policy with its own termination condition), typically hand-designed or pre-trained separately. This note exists because hand-specifying useful options doesn't scale to complex domains - FuN and HIRO exist to make the high-level/low-level interface itself learnable: the high-level policy outputs a continuous 'goal' (a direction in a learned representation space, or a target state), and the low-level policy learns to achieve whatever goals the high-level policy proposes, with both levels trained end-to-end.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.how_it_works: FuN structures the agent as a 'Manager' operating at a slower timescale that outputs goal directions in a learned latent state-representation space, and a 'Worker' operating at the fast timescale that receives an intrinsic reward for moving the state representation in the direction the Manager specified (measured via cosine similarity between the actual state-representation change and the Manager's goal direction) - the Manager learns to set useful directions via its own (slower) policy gradient, while the Worker learns to follow directions via the intrinsic reward, with the two levels using different effective time horizons. HIRO instead has a high-level policy periodically output an explicit goal state (a target for the low-level policy to reach within a fixed horizon), with the low-level policy trained off-policy with a dense reward based on distance-to-goal; HIRO's key innovation is an off-policy correction that relabels past high-level transitions' goals to account for the fact that the low-level policy's behavior changes over training (without this correction, off-policy high-level updates would use stale, inconsistent goal-conditioned data).
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.use_when: Long-horizon tasks with natural temporal/spatial structure where a 'navigate toward a sub-goal' decomposition makes sense (robot navigation with manager setting waypoints, worker executing low-level locomotion); tasks where hand-designing discrete options is impractical but a continuous learned goal/sub-goal interface is natural; when you want to combine the sample-efficiency benefits of off-policy learning (HIRO) with hierarchical temporal abstraction.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.avoid_when: Short-horizon tasks where the credit-assignment/exploration benefits of hierarchy don't outweigh the added complexity of training two coupled policies; tasks where a natural 'goal space' for the high-level policy to operate in isn't obvious (e.g., discrete combinatorial action spaces where 'directions' or 'target states' don't have clean meaning) - classical discrete options or flat RL may be simpler.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.what_goes_wrong: Training two policies simultaneously creates a moving-target problem - the low-level policy's behavior changes as it learns, making the high-level policy's effective 'action space' (what goals lead to what outcomes) non-stationary, which HIRO's off-policy goal-relabeling specifically addresses but doesn't fully eliminate; FuN's cosine-similarity intrinsic reward can be gamed by the Worker finding directions that are easy to move in but don't correspond to meaningful task progress, especially early in training when the learned state representation isn't yet meaningful; both approaches add substantial implementation complexity (two networks, two reward signals, careful timescale tuning) compared to flat RL, and the benefits often only materialize on sufficiently long-horizon, structured tasks.
9|⚪ T3 🔬 Multi-Agent (Complete)|Multi-Ag.real_example: HIRO was demonstrated on long-horizon simulated ant/robot navigation tasks (e.g., navigating a maze) where a high-level policy proposes waypoint goals every few steps and a low-level policy learns general 'reach this nearby target' locomotion - achieving better sample efficiency and performance than flat off-policy RL (TD3/SAC) on tasks requiring the agent to traverse long distances through structured environments.
